Wikipedia — Gibbs free energy (the underlying ΔG)

atoms.art_prompt: wild-type vs mutant folded states on a shifted free-energy scale

quiz.prompt: What does ΔΔG measure?
quiz.answer: The change in folding free energy caused by a mutation (mutant minus wild type).

quiz.prompt: Can a stabilizing mutation still cause disease? Explain.
quiz.answer: Yes — stability and aggregation/function are different observables; a mutation can stabilize the fold yet promote aggregation or impair function.

quiz.prompt: The folded:unfolded population ratio is K = exp(−ΔG_fold/RT). A point mutation has ΔΔG = +1.4 kcal/mol (destabilizing). By roughly what factor does it shift the folded:unfolded ratio at 298 K, and why that number?
quiz.answer: The ratio changes by exp(−ΔΔG/RT). With RT ≈ 0.59 kcal/mol, ΔΔG/RT = 1.4/0.59 ≈ 2.3 = ln 10, so K drops by a factor of ≈ 10 — the fold is ~10× less populated. (≈1.4 kcal/mol per decade is the recurring 'one log unit' rule of thumb.)

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Swap just one of a protein's amino-acid beads for a different one. Does the protein now hold its shape better or worse? That "change in the change" is called **ΔΔG**. ("Wild type" means the normal, unmutated version; a "mutant" is the changed one.) It is the single most-used number in protein engineering and in judging whether a genetic variant is likely harmful.

### Precisely

$$\Delta\Delta G = \Delta G_{\text{fold}}^{\text{mut}} - \Delta G_{\text{fold}}^{\text{wt}},$$

the difference between the mutant's and wild type's **folding free energy**. It is a change *of a change* — hence the double delta. With the common sign convention (defining $\Delta G_{\text{fold}}$ as the stability of the folded state), a **positive ΔΔG means the mutation destabilizes** the fold; negative means it stabilizes. Units are kcal/mol.

### Worked example

A surface salt-bridge mutation might give $\Delta\Delta G \approx +1$ kcal/mol — modestly destabilizing. Because populations depend exponentially on free energy, a $+1.8$ kcal/mol destabilization at 310 K shifts the folded:unfolded ratio by $e^{1.8/0.6} = e^{3}\approx 20$-fold toward unfolded. Burying a charge or creating a cavity can cost several kcal/mol, enough to unfold the protein at body temperature.

### Why it's true / how it works

ΔΔG is measured by determining $\Delta G_{\text{fold}}$ for both proteins from their **two-state** melting curves (vs temperature or denaturant) and subtracting. Because $\Delta G_{\text{fold}}$ is itself a small difference of large numbers, ΔΔG isolates the *local* energetic effect of one residue change — lost contacts, new clashes, altered burial of hydrophobic surface.

### Where it connects

It builds directly on **two-state folding**, **Gibbs free energy**, and the **hydrophobic effect**; it is the target of FEP/alchemical **free-energy methods** and ML predictors, and the basis of variant-effect interpretation in disease genetics.

### Watch out

Stability is **not** the same observable as **aggregation** or **function**. A mutation can *stabilize* the fold yet still cause disease by promoting clumping or by killing catalytic activity. Also, sign conventions differ between software tools — always confirm which direction a program calls "destabilizing" before trusting its number.

### Numbers & nuance

Scale intuition at 310 K: since populations depend on $e^{-\Delta\Delta G/k_BT}$, a $+1.4$ kcal/mol destabilization shifts the folded:unfolded ratio ~10-fold, and $+4$ kcal/mol can unfold a marginally stable protein outright (recall total stabilities are only ~5–15 kcal/mol). Common destabilizers: creating a buried cavity (~1–2 kcal/mol per lost methyl contact), burying an uncompensated charge, or introducing a backbone strain; common stabilizers: improved core packing, added salt bridges on the surface, proline substitutions that reduce unfolded-state entropy. Because thermodynamic cycles let you compute $\Delta\Delta G$ by *alchemically* mutating residue identity in simulation, FEP-based $\Delta\Delta G$ predictions now reach ~1 kcal/mol accuracy for well-behaved cases — competitive with experiment. The broader lesson is to match the *measured* quantity to the *question*: folding stability, aggregation propensity, and catalytic activity are three distinct observables, and a mutation can move them in different directions — so a ΔΔG number alone never settles whether a variant is benign or pathogenic without knowing which property actually limits function in vivo.

atoms.title: Binding & the dissociation constant
atoms.summary: K_d is the ligand concentration at which a site is half-occupied — the universal currency of molecular recognition.

depths.eli5: A 'ligand' is just any small molecule that sticks to a protein (a drug, a hormone, oxygen). Slowly add more and more ligand to a pot of protein. The K_d is the ligand concentration at which exactly half the protein molecules have something stuck to them. A small K_d means you only needed a tiny amount of ligand to reach half — so it sticks tightly. Big K_d, weak sticking.
depths.core: From the law of mass action (the rule that reaction rates depend on how much of each ingredient is present), the fraction of sites occupied, θ, follows a hyperbola: θ = [L]/(K_d + [L]), where [L] is free-ligand concentration. Plug in [L] = K_d and you get θ = 0.5 — half occupied. K_d converts directly to an energy via ΔG° = RT·ln K_d, so a binder 10 times tighter is about 1.4 kcal/mol more stable. K_d is the universal currency for how strongly two molecules recognize each other.
depths.deep: K_d also equals k_off/k_on — the ratio of the 'off' rate (how fast bound ligand falls off) to the 'on' rate (how fast it attaches). This ties the equilibrium (K_d) to the kinetics (the rates). Many drugs are actually optimized on a slow k_off — long 'residence time' on the target — rather than on K_d alone.

atoms.note: Rough scale: nanomolar (nM) K_d ≈ tight binding, micromolar (µM) ≈ moderate, millimolar (mM) ≈ weak. Every 10× change in K_d ≈ 1.4 kcal/mol at body temperature (310 K).

quiz.prompt: What does K_d equal in terms of occupancy?
quiz.answer: The free-ligand concentration at which the binding site is half-occupied (θ = 0.5).

quiz.prompt: Show that occupancy is θ = [L]/(K_d+[L]).
quiz.answer: From K_d = [P][L]/[PL], θ = [PL]/([P]+[PL]) = [L]/(K_d+[L]) after substituting [PL] = [P][L]/K_d.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **ligand** is any small molecule that sticks to a protein — a drug, a hormone, oxygen. Slowly add more and more ligand to a pot of protein. The **K_d** is the ligand concentration at which exactly half the protein molecules have something stuck to them. A *small* K_d means you needed only a tiny amount of ligand to reach half-occupancy — so it binds *tightly*. A big K_d means weak binding.

### Precisely

From the **law of mass action**, the dissociation reaction $PL \rightleftharpoons P + L$ has equilibrium constant

$$K_d = \frac{[P][L]}{[PL]},$$

and the **fractional occupancy** of sites follows a hyperbola:

$$\theta = \frac{[L]}{K_d + [L]}.$$

Set $[L]=K_d$ and $\theta = 0.5$ — half occupied. $K_d$ has units of concentration (M); $\Delta G^\circ = RT\ln K_d$ converts it to an energy.

### Worked example

A drug with $K_d = 10$ nM means half its target is bound when free drug reaches 10 nM. Compare a weaker $K_d = 100$ nM binder: the 10-fold tighter drug is more stable by $\Delta\Delta G = RT\ln(10) = 0.6\times2.3 \approx 1.4$ kcal/mol. As a scale: nanomolar $K_d$ = tight, micromolar = moderate, millimolar = weak — and every 10× change in $K_d$ is ~1.4 kcal/mol at 310 K.

### Why it's true / how it works

Start from $K_d = [P][L]/[PL]$, so $[PL] = [P][L]/K_d$. Occupancy is $\theta = [PL]/([P]+[PL])$. Substituting and cancelling $[P]$ gives $\theta = [L]/(K_d+[L])$ — the **Langmuir** binding isotherm. The half-saturation point falls exactly at $[L]=K_d$, which is why $K_d$ is reported as *the* affinity.

### Where it connects

$K_d$ is the foundation of **cooperativity** (the Hill equation), **MWC/KNF allostery**, enzyme **Michaelis–Menten** ($K_M$ is a binding-like constant), and **FRET**/tweezer affinity measurements. Via $\Delta G^\circ = RT\ln K_d$ it ties to **Gibbs free energy**.

### Why it's true / how it works (kinetics)

$K_d = k_{\text{off}}/k_{\text{on}}$ — the ratio of the dissociation rate to the association rate — linking equilibrium to **kinetics**. Many drugs are optimized for a slow $k_{\text{off}}$ (long **residence time**) rather than $K_d$ alone.

### Watch out The common pitfall: confusing **total** ligand with **free** ligand $[L]$. The hyperbola uses *free* ligand; when protein concentration is comparable to $K_d$, ligand depletion makes the apparent affinity look weaker than it is.

### Numbers & nuance

Affinity-to-energy ladder at 310 K ($RT\approx0.6$ kcal/mol, so each 10× in $K_d$ is ~1.4 kcal/mol): mM $\approx 4$ kcal/mol (weak, metabolite-level), µM $\approx 8$ kcal/mol (moderate), nM $\approx 12$ kcal/mol (tight drug/antibody), pM $\approx 16$ kcal/mol (very tight). Association rates $k_{\text{on}}$ rarely exceed the diffusion limit (~$10^8$–$10^9\,\mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}$), so very high affinity is usually achieved by a very *slow* off-rate $k_{\text{off}}$ rather than a faster on-rate. The residence time $1/k_{\text{off}}$ — how long a complex stays together — often predicts drug efficacy better than $K_d$, because biological effect depends on *how long* the target is occupied, not just the equilibrium fraction.

atoms.title: Cooperativity & the Hill equation
atoms.summary: When binding one ligand helps the next, the binding curve sharpens from a hyperbola into a switch.

depths.eli5: Some proteins have several binding spots. If grabbing the first ligand makes the protein hungrier for the next one, then once binding starts it quickly snowballs. The result is a sharp switch: almost nothing bound, then suddenly almost everything bound, over a narrow range of concentration — instead of the gentle, gradual curve you'd get from independent spots.
depths.core: The Hill coefficient n is a single number summarizing cooperativity. n = 1 means the sites act independently (ordinary hyperbola, no teamwork); n > 1 means positive cooperativity — binding one ligand boosts the affinity for the next — giving an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve. Hemoglobin binding oxygen (n ≈ 2.8 across its four sites) is the classic example, and it's what makes oxygen pickup and delivery efficient.
depths.deep: The Hill equation is 'phenomenological' — a useful curve-fit rather than a mechanism. The theoretical maximum n equals the number of sites (perfect all-or-none binding). To explain WHERE cooperativity actually comes from, you need mechanistic models like MWC (concerted) and KNF (sequential).

atoms.art_prompt: a hyperbola morphing into a steep sigmoid as cooperativity increases

quiz.prompt: What does a Hill coefficient n > 1 indicate?
quiz.answer: Positive cooperativity — binding one ligand increases affinity for the next, giving a sigmoidal (switch-like) curve.

quiz.prompt: Why is cooperative O₂ binding useful for hemoglobin?
quiz.answer: The sigmoidal curve lets it load O₂ in the lungs and unload it in tissues over a small change in O₂ pressure.

quiz.prompt: From θ = [L]ⁿ/(K_d + [L]ⁿ), show that a plot of log(θ/(1−θ)) versus log[L] is a straight line, and identify its slope.
quiz.answer: 1−θ = K_d/(K_d + [L]ⁿ), so θ/(1−θ) = [L]ⁿ/K_d. Taking logs: log(θ/(1−θ)) = n·log[L] − log K_d — linear in log[L] with slope n, the Hill coefficient. (This 'Hill plot' is how n is measured experimentally.)

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Some proteins have several binding spots. If grabbing the first ligand makes the protein *hungrier* for the next, then once binding starts it snowballs. The result is a sharp switch — almost nothing bound, then suddenly almost everything bound, over a narrow concentration range — instead of the gentle hyperbola you'd get from independent spots.

### Precisely

The **Hill equation** describes cooperative occupancy with a single empirical exponent $n$, the **Hill coefficient**:

$$\theta = \frac{[L]^n}{K_d + [L]^n}.$$

$n=1$ recovers the ordinary non-cooperative hyperbola (independent sites). $n>1$ means **positive cooperativity** — binding one ligand raises affinity for the next — producing an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve. $n<1$ signals negative cooperativity. The steepness of the switch grows with $n$.

### Worked example

**Haemoglobin** binds oxygen with $n\approx 2.8$ across its four sites. This sigmoidal curve lets it load O₂ efficiently in the high-pressure lungs and *unload* it sharply in low-pressure tissues — a switch a simple hyperbola could never achieve. The "P50" (the O₂ pressure giving half-saturation) plays the role of an apparent $K_d$, and the steepness around it is what cooperativity buys.

### Why it's true / how it works

The Hill equation is the limiting case of **perfectly concerted** binding: if all $n$ sites must fill simultaneously, the occupancy is exactly $[L]^n/(K_d+[L]^n)$. Real proteins fill sites one at a time, so the *measured* Hill coefficient is always **less than** the number of sites — it is an *effective* cooperativity, bounded above by the site count.

### Where it connects

It sharpens the **binding ($K_d$)** picture into a switch and motivates the mechanistic models **MWC** (concerted T↔R) and **KNF** (sequential induced fit) that explain *where* the cooperativity comes from. The same sigmoidal mathematics appears in **signal transduction** ultrasensitivity.

### Watch out

The Hill equation is **phenomenological** — a curve fit, not a mechanism. A fitted $n$ is *not* literally the number of binding sites; it is a lower bound and an index of cooperativity. Reading $n=2.8$ as "2.8 sites" (haemoglobin has four) is the classic error.

### Numbers & nuance

Read the Hill coefficient as a *lower bound* on the number of interacting sites and an index of switch sharpness: $n=1$ is a plain hyperbola spanning ~81-fold ligand concentration from 10% to 90% saturation, while $n=4$ compresses that same 10→90% transition into only ~$81^{1/4}\approx 3$-fold concentration — a near-digital switch. Haemoglobin's $n\approx2.8$ (not 4, despite four sites) shows real cooperativity is never perfectly concerted. The same mathematics describes ultrasensitive *signaling* responses, where an apparent high Hill coefficient can arise from cascades or zero-order effects rather than literal multi-site binding — so a steep dose–response curve indicates a switch, but not necessarily allosteric binding. In short, the Hill coefficient is best read as a *dimensionless sharpness index* of the response, with its theoretical ceiling equal to the number of interacting sites and its observed value always falling short of that ceiling for any real, sequentially-binding system.

atoms.title: MWC allostery
atoms.summary: Cooperativity from a concerted switch between a tense (T) and relaxed (R) state of the whole assembly.

depths.eli5: Picture a protein made of identical pieces that always flip shape together, all at once, between a 'tense' shape (bad at grabbing ligand) and a 'relaxed' shape (good at grabbing ligand). Both shapes are always present in some mix. When ligand is around it sticks better to the relaxed shape, so it tips the whole crowd toward relaxed — and that tipping is where the cooperative, switch-like behavior comes from.
depths.core: The Monod–Wyman–Changeux (MWC) model: an 'oligomer' (a protein built from several identical subunits) already exists in two interconverting states — T (tense, low ligand affinity) and R (relaxed, high affinity) — in equilibrium, even before any ligand arrives. Because ligand binds the R state better, binding shifts the population toward R. This 'concerted' (all-subunits-together) switch produces cooperativity without any 'induced fit', where binding would reshape one site at a time.
depths.deep: MWC (concerted) and KNF (sequential) are the two classic frameworks for allostery (regulation at a distance). Real proteins often fall between them. MWC's idea that ligand simply selects a pre-existing shape — 'conformational selection' — connects directly to modern ensemble and energy-landscape thinking.

atoms.art_prompt: a symmetric oligomer toggling concertedly between tense and relaxed states

quiz.prompt: In MWC, where does cooperativity come from?
quiz.answer: From a pre-existing equilibrium between a low-affinity (T) and high-affinity (R) state; ligand binding shifts the whole assembly toward R.

quiz.prompt: How does MWC differ from the KNF (induced-fit) model?
quiz.answer: MWC is concerted (all subunits switch together, conformational selection); KNF is sequential (each binding event induces a local change).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Picture a protein built from identical pieces that always flip shape *together*, all at once, between a **tense** form (poor at grabbing ligand) and a **relaxed** form (good at grabbing ligand). Both forms are always present in some mix, even with no ligand around. When ligand appears it sticks better to the relaxed form, so it tips the whole crowd toward relaxed — and that collective tipping is the source of cooperativity.

### Precisely

The **Monod–Wyman–Changeux (MWC)** model describes an **oligomer** (several identical subunits) that pre-exists in two interconverting, symmetric states: **T** (tense, low ligand affinity) and **R** (relaxed, high affinity). Three parameters define it: the **allosteric constant** $L = [T_0]/[R_0]$ (the T:R ratio with no ligand bound), and the dissociation constants $K_T$ and $K_R$ ($K_R < K_T$). The whole assembly switches **concertedly** — all subunits share the same conformation, preserving symmetry.

### Worked example

Suppose $L$ is large (T heavily favoured when empty) and $K_R \ll K_T$. The first few ligands bind preferentially to the rare R molecules; each binding event makes R relatively more stable, shifting the equilibrium and exposing more high-affinity R sites. The net effect is that affinity *rises* as occupancy rises — a sigmoidal curve — even though no individual site changed its intrinsic $K_R$.

### Why it's true / how it works

MWC produces cooperativity by **conformational selection**: ligand does not *reshape* a site (no induced fit), it *selects* and stabilizes a pre-existing high-affinity state from the ensemble. Mass action then drags the population toward R. This is why MWC is called "concerted" — symmetry is never broken.

### Where it connects

MWC is one of the two classic allostery frameworks; its sibling is **KNF** (sequential induced fit). Real proteins often lie between them. MWC's "ligand selects a pre-existing state" idea connects directly to modern **energy-landscape** and **ensemble** thinking and to the **conformational selection** vs induced-fit debate.

### Watch out

MWC assumes **symmetry is conserved** (no mixed T/R oligomers), which is an idealization — many real allosteric proteins violate it. MWC explains positive cooperativity naturally but, in its pure symmetric form, *cannot* produce **negative** cooperativity, whereas KNF can.

### Numbers & nuance

MWC has just three parameters — $L$ (the T:R ratio with zero ligand), $K_T$, and $K_R$ — yet reproduces haemoglobin's full oxygen-binding curve. The mechanism is **conformational selection**: even before ligand arrives, both T and R exist, and ligand merely *shifts the pre-existing equilibrium* by binding R better. This connects to a modern, experimentally supported view — proteins are dynamic ensembles, and "allostery" is often a redistribution of populations rather than a mechanical lever. Effectors that bind T (lowering affinity, like 2,3-BPG in haemoglobin) or R (raising it) tune the curve by changing $L$. MWC's clean prediction is that it can produce *positive* cooperativity and effector tuning but, in its symmetric form, never *negative* cooperativity — that requires KNF.

atoms.title: Michaelis–Menten kinetics
atoms.summary: Enzyme rate rises with substrate then saturates; K_M and V_max characterize the enzyme.

depths.eli5: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction, and the 'substrate' is the stuff it works on. Feed an enzyme more substrate and it works faster — but only up to a point. Once every enzyme molecule is busy all the time, piling on more substrate can't help; it's already going flat out. The speed levels off at a ceiling.
depths.core: Assuming the amount of enzyme–substrate complex holds roughly steady (the steady-state, or Briggs–Haldane, assumption), the starting reaction rate v traces a hyperbola as substrate [S] increases. K_M (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration that gives half the maximum rate, V_max — loosely a measure of how readily the enzyme grabs substrate. The ratio k_cat/K_M (k_cat being the top turnover speed per enzyme) is the 'specificity constant' used to compare how good different enzymes are.
depths.deep: k_cat/K_M can't exceed the speed at which enzyme and substrate find each other by diffusion (~10^8–10^9 per molar per second). Enzymes that hit this ceiling are called 'catalytically perfect' — directly linking enzyme kinetics back to the physics of diffusion.

atoms.art_prompt: a saturating rate-vs-substrate hyperbola with Km at half Vmax

quiz.prompt: What does K_M represent on the rate curve?
quiz.answer: The substrate concentration giving half the maximum rate (V_max/2).

quiz.prompt: What assumption yields the Michaelis–Menten form, and what is the specificity constant?
quiz.answer: Steady state for [ES] (d[ES]/dt ≈ 0); specificity constant is k_cat/K_M.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

An **enzyme** is a protein catalyst that speeds a reaction by binding its **substrate** (the starting molecule) and lowering the barrier to convert it to product. Feed an enzyme more and more substrate and its rate climbs — but only up to a ceiling. Once every enzyme molecule is busy at all times, adding more substrate cannot help: the enzyme is **saturated**, and it runs at top speed.

### Precisely

For the scheme $E + S \rightleftharpoons ES \rightarrow E + P$, the initial reaction velocity is

$$v = \frac{V_{\max}[S]}{K_M + [S]},$$

a hyperbola in substrate concentration $[S]$. $V_{\max} = k_{\text{cat}}[E]_{\text{total}}$ is the saturating top speed; $k_{\text{cat}}$ (the **turnover number**) is how many substrates one enzyme converts per second when saturated. $K_M$, the **Michaelis constant** (units M), is the substrate concentration giving half-maximal rate, $v = V_{\max}/2$.

### Worked example

If $K_M = 50\ \mu$M and $V_{\max} = 100\ \mu$M/s, then at $[S] = 50\ \mu$M, $v = 50$ μM/s (half max). At $[S]=500\ \mu$M ($10\,K_M$), $v = 100\times500/(50+500) \approx 91$ μM/s — close to saturation. The **specificity constant** $k_{\text{cat}}/K_M$ governs efficiency at low substrate and is bounded above by the diffusion-limited encounter rate (~$10^8$–$10^9\,\mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}$).

### Why it's true / how it works

Assume the intermediate $ES$ reaches a **steady state** (its concentration stays roughly constant: formation balances breakdown). Setting $d[ES]/dt = 0$ gives $[ES] = [E][S]/K_M$ with $K_M = (k_{-1}+k_{\text{cat}})/k_1$. The product-formation rate $v = k_{\text{cat}}[ES]$ then rearranges to the Michaelis–Menten hyperbola.

### Where it connects

$K_M$ is a binding-like constant rooted in **K_d**; $k_{\text{cat}}$ connects to **transition-state theory (Eyring)** via the catalytic barrier; cooperative enzymes follow **Hill/MWC/KNF**; the diffusion ceiling is the **Smoluchowski** rate.

### Watch out

$K_M$ is **not** simply the substrate dissociation constant — it equals $(k_{-1}+k_{\text{cat}})/k_1$, which only reduces to $K_d$ when catalysis is slow compared to unbinding. And the equation describes *initial* velocity (before product accumulates and before substrate is depleted); applying it to late-stage time courses is a common mistake.

### Numbers & nuance

Interpret the two constants separately: $k_{\text{cat}}$ (turnover number) ranges from ~1/s for slow enzymes to >$10^5$/s for fast ones; $K_M$ (the half-saturation substrate concentration, units M) often roughly matches physiological substrate levels, so enzymes operate on the steep part of their curve and stay responsive. The **specificity constant** $k_{\text{cat}}/K_M$ measures catalytic efficiency at low substrate and is capped by the diffusion limit (~$10^8$–$10^9\,\mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}$); enzymes near that ceiling (e.g. triosephosphate isomerase, catalase) are called "catalytically perfect." Inhibitors are classified by *which* parameter they change — competitive inhibitors raise apparent $K_M$, uncompetitive lower both, and non-competitive lower $V_{\max}$ — a diagnostic read directly off Michaelis–Menten plots. A final practical note: because the equation describes *initial* velocity (before product accumulates and substrate depletes), it is fit to early-time data or to a Lineweaver–Burk / Eadie–Hofstee linearization; applying it to full progress curves without accounting for product inhibition and reverse reaction is a common source of error in reported kinetic constants.

atoms.title: Transition-state theory (Eyring)
atoms.summary: Reaction rate is set by the free-energy barrier to a transition state — the bridge from thermodynamics to kinetics.

depths.eli5: Between the starting molecules and the finished product there's an energy 'hill' to climb. The reaction can only happen as fast as it's easy to get over that hill. A tall hill means the reaction crawls; a low hill means it races. The very top of the hill — the most awkward, halfway-rearranged moment — is the 'transition state'.
depths.core: Eyring's equation relates a reaction's rate constant to the activation free energy ΔG‡ — the height of the energy barrier up to the transition state (the ‡ symbol marks 'of the transition state'). The leading factor k_BT/h (about 6×10^12 per second at body temperature, where h is Planck's constant) sets the basic 'attempt frequency'. This explains two things at once: catalysis means lowering the barrier, and reaction rates are extremely sensitive to temperature.
depths.deep: An enzyme speeds a reaction by binding the awkward transition state more tightly than it binds the comfortable starting substrate — Linus Pauling's insight. That is also the rationale for 'transition-state-analog' drugs: molecules shaped like the transition state jam the enzyme by binding where it grips hardest.

atoms.art_prompt: a reaction coordinate with a barrier at the transition state, lowered by a catalyst

quiz.prompt: What single quantity sets the rate in transition-state theory?
quiz.answer: The activation free energy ΔG‡ — the barrier height to the transition state.

quiz.prompt: In one sentence, how does an enzyme speed a reaction in this framework?
quiz.answer: By preferentially stabilizing (binding) the transition state, lowering ΔG‡.

quiz.prompt: From k = (k_BT/h)·exp(−ΔG‡/k_BT), derive how much the activation free energy must drop to speed a reaction 10-fold at 298 K (treat the prefactor as constant).
quiz.answer: k₂/k₁ = exp[−(ΔG₂‡−ΔG₁‡)/RT]; setting this to 10 gives Δ(ΔG‡) = −RT·ln 10 ≈ −0.59×2.3 ≈ −1.4 kcal/mol. So every ~1.4 kcal/mol of barrier lowering buys roughly one decade of rate.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

To turn into product, reacting molecules must first climb to an awkward, high-energy halfway arrangement — the **transition state**, the unstable peak between reactants and products. The taller that peak, the rarer the thermal kick big enough to reach it, and the slower the reaction. Rate is governed by the *height of the hill*, not by how favourable the destination is.

### Precisely

**Transition-state theory** (Eyring) gives the rate constant

$$k = \frac{k_BT}{h}\,e^{-\Delta G^{\ddagger}/k_BT},$$

where $\Delta G^{\ddagger}$ is the **activation free energy** (the free-energy height of the transition state above reactants), $h$ is Planck's constant, and the prefactor $k_BT/h \approx 6\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at 300 K is a universal attempt frequency. Splitting $\Delta G^{\ddagger}=\Delta H^{\ddagger}-T\Delta S^{\ddagger}$ separates the enthalpic barrier from the entropic cost of organizing the transition state.

### Worked example

A barrier of $\Delta G^{\ddagger} = 15$ kcal/mol at 310 K gives $e^{-15/0.6} = e^{-25} \approx 1.4\times10^{-11}$. Multiply by the prefactor $\sim 6\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ to get $k \approx 85\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Add just 2.8 kcal/mol to the barrier and $k$ drops ~100-fold — illustrating why enzymes, which *lower* $\Delta G^{\ddagger}$ by binding the transition state tightest, achieve enormous rate accelerations.

### Why it's true / how it works

The theory assumes reactants are in quasi-equilibrium with an activated complex at the barrier top, and that complexes crossing the saddle proceed to product. The equilibrium population at the barrier is Boltzmann-weighted, $\propto e^{-\Delta G^{\ddagger}/k_BT}$, and the crossing frequency supplies the $k_BT/h$ prefactor.

### Where it connects

It is the kinetic bridge from **Gibbs free energy** to rates, underlies **Michaelis–Menten** $k_{\text{cat}}$ and enzyme catalysis, and is refined by **Kramers theory**, which adds the friction-dependent prefactor that Eyring's idealized $k_BT/h$ omits. Compare with **Arrhenius**, its empirical cousin.

### Watch out

The clean $k_BT/h$ prefactor assumes barrier crossings never recross — but in viscous, friction-rich biological solvents they do, so **Kramers** corrects the prefactor downward (the **transmission coefficient** $\kappa<1$). Treating $\Delta G^{\ddagger}$ as the *reaction's* $\Delta G$ is also wrong: the barrier height sets rate, the reaction $\Delta G$ sets equilibrium.

### Numbers & nuance

The prefactor $k_BT/h \approx 6.2\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at 300 K is the universal "attempt frequency." A rough rule: at 310 K, every extra $1.4$ kcal/mol of barrier slows a reaction ~10-fold (since $e^{1.4/0.6}\approx10$). So a 17 kcal/mol barrier gives roughly seconds-to-minutes timescales, while a 5 kcal/mol barrier is microsecond-fast. Enzymes accelerate reactions by *binding the transition state more tightly than the substrate*, effectively lowering $\Delta G^{\ddagger}$ — a 10⁶-fold rate enhancement corresponds to ~8 kcal/mol of differential transition-state stabilization. Splitting $\Delta G^{\ddagger} = \Delta H^{\ddagger} - T\Delta S^{\ddagger}$ via an Eyring plot ($\ln(k/T)$ vs $1/T$) separates the enthalpic barrier from the entropic cost of organizing the activated complex. The practical upshot for biology: because rate depends exponentially on the barrier, evolution and drug design tune $\Delta G^{\ddagger}$ — not the overall reaction $\Delta G$ — to set timescales, and the same exponential sensitivity is why modest changes in temperature or a single active-site mutation can swing a rate by orders of magnitude.

atoms.title: Diffusion — Fick's laws
atoms.summary: Matter flows down concentration gradients; the diffusion coefficient D sets how fast.

depths.eli5: Drop a bit of dye in still water and it slowly spreads out from where it's crowded toward where there's none — no stirring needed. Fick's law just says: the steeper the difference in crowding from one spot to the next (the 'gradient'), the faster stuff flows to even it out. 'Flux' is simply the amount of stuff crossing an area each second.
depths.core: Fick's first law says the diffusive flux J (how much material crosses a unit area per second) is proportional to the concentration gradient ∇c (how sharply concentration changes with position), pointing from high to low. Combine it with conservation of matter (nothing vanishes) and you get the diffusion equation, ∂c/∂t = D∇²c, which predicts how a concentration evolves over time. The diffusion coefficient D measures how fast a given molecule spreads. Diffusion is how molecules find their targets inside cells and it sets the speed limit of any transport that isn't actively stirred.
depths.deep: Diffusion is the large-scale face of random molecular jiggling. The very same D shows up in the microscopic mean-square-displacement law (see random walk) and in the Einstein relation that ties it to temperature and friction.

LibreTexts Chemistry — Physical & Theoretical Chemistry texts

atoms.art_prompt: molecules streaming down a smooth concentration gradient

quiz.prompt: What does Fick's first law relate?
quiz.answer: Diffusive flux J to the concentration gradient ∇c (J = −D∇c).

quiz.prompt: Write the diffusion equation that follows from Fick's law plus conservation of mass.
quiz.answer: ∂c/∂t = D∇²c.

quiz.prompt: At steady state with constant D, what equation does c obey, and what is the concentration profile and flux between two faces held at c₁ and c₂ a distance L apart?
quiz.answer: Steady state means ∂c/∂t = 0, so the diffusion equation D∇²c = 0 reduces to Laplace's equation ∇²c = 0. In 1-D that forces a linear profile c(x) = c₁ + (c₂−c₁)x/L; the flux is constant, J = −D·dc/dx = D(c₁−c₂)/L.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Drop ink in still water and it spreads from where it is concentrated to where it is not, evening out on its own — no stirring required. The driving "force" is just statistics: random molecular wandering inevitably carries more particles out of crowded regions than into them. Matter flows **down concentration gradients**, and the steeper the gradient, the faster the flow.

### Precisely

**Fick's first law** relates the diffusive **flux** $J$ (amount crossing unit area per unit time) to the concentration gradient:

$$J = -D\,\nabla c,$$

where $c$ is concentration, $\nabla c$ its spatial gradient, and $D$ the **diffusion coefficient** (units m²/s) — a measure of how fast a species spreads. The minus sign means flow points *down* the gradient. Combining this with mass conservation gives **Fick's second law**, the diffusion equation $\partial c/\partial t = D\,\nabla^2 c$, which predicts how concentration profiles evolve in time.

### Worked example

A small molecule in water has $D \approx 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m^2/s} = 1\ \mu\mathrm{m^2/ms}$. The time to diffuse a distance $L$ scales as $t \sim L^2/(2D)$. Crossing a 10 μm cell takes $t \sim (10^{-5})^2/(2\times10^{-9}) \approx 0.05$ s — fast. But crossing a 1 mm tissue takes $\sim 500$ s — minutes — which is why large organisms need circulatory systems rather than relying on diffusion.

### Why it's true / how it works

Fick's law is the **macroscopic** face of microscopic randomness. If each molecule performs a **random walk**, regions of higher concentration simply have more random-walkers available to step outward than inward, producing a net flux proportional to the gradient. The same constant $D$ appears in both the macroscopic flux law and the microscopic mean-square displacement $\langle x^2\rangle = 2Dt$.

### Where it connects

Fick's laws emerge from the **random walk**, set the magnitude of $D$ through the **Einstein–Stokes** relation, cap reaction speeds at the **Smoluchowski** diffusion limit, and govern oxygen and nutrient transport, **reaction–diffusion** pattern formation, and ion movement underlying the **Nernst/GHK** potentials.

### Watch out

The $L^2$ scaling is the crucial, counterintuitive point: doubling the distance *quadruples* the time. Diffusion is wonderfully fast over microns but hopeless over millimetres. Also, Fick's law assumes no bulk flow, no electric forces, and dilute, non-interacting solute — charged species need the extended **Nernst–Planck** equation.

### Numbers & nuance

Diffusion coefficients in water at room temperature: small molecules ~$10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$ (~$10^3\,\mu\mathrm{m^2/s}$), proteins ~$10^{-10}$–$10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$, organelles slower still. The diffusion time over a length $L$ is $\tau \sim L^2/(2D)$ in 1D (or $L^2/(6D)$ in 3D), and the $L^2$ scaling is decisive: 1 µm in ~0.5 ms, 100 µm in ~5 s, 1 mm in ~8 min. This is precisely why bacteria (~1 µm) can rely on diffusion for everything, single large cells need stirring or active transport, and multicellular organisms require circulatory and respiratory systems to bridge the millimetre-and-beyond gap that diffusion alone cannot service in useful time.

atoms.title: Einstein–Stokes relation
atoms.summary: Diffusion, temperature, viscosity, and size are linked — bigger and stickier means slower.

depths.eli5: How fast a tiny particle wanders around in a liquid depends on four things: how warm it is (warmer = more jiggle), how thick the liquid is (honey vs water), and how big the particle is. Small things in thin, warm liquid zip around; big things in thick, cold liquid barely crawl. This formula ties all of that together.
depths.core: The Einstein relation D = k_BT/γ says the diffusion coefficient D equals the thermal energy k_BT divided by the friction (drag) coefficient γ. For a sphere of radius r moving through a liquid of viscosity η (its 'thickness' or resistance to flow), Stokes' law gives γ = 6πηr. Put them together: D = k_BT/(6πηr). This lets you estimate how fast a molecule diffuses from its size, or work out its size from a measured D (as in dynamic light scattering).
depths.deep: This is a 'fluctuation–dissipation' result: the very same friction γ that slows a particle down (dissipation) also sets the strength of the random thermal kicks that keep it moving (fluctuation). Drag and noise are two faces of one coin — you can't have one without the other at a given temperature.

quiz.prompt: How does diffusion coefficient depend on particle radius and viscosity?
quiz.answer: Inversely on both: D = kT/(6πηr) — bigger or more viscous means slower diffusion.

quiz.prompt: From the Einstein relation D = kT/γ and Stokes drag, get D for a sphere.
quiz.answer: Substitute γ = 6πηr: D = kT/(6πηr).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

How fast a molecule jiggles through a fluid depends on three sensible things: how hard the thermal kicks are (temperature), how thick and sticky the fluid is (viscosity), and how big the molecule is (size). Hotter means faster; thicker fluid or bigger particle means slower. The Einstein–Stokes relation packages all three into one clean formula.

### Precisely

For a spherical particle of radius $r$ in a fluid of viscosity $\eta$ at temperature $T$,

$$D = \frac{k_BT}{6\pi\eta r},$$

where $D$ is the **diffusion coefficient** (m²/s) and $6\pi\eta r$ is the **Stokes drag** coefficient for a sphere. Bigger ($r\uparrow$) and stickier ($\eta\uparrow$) means slower diffusion; warmer ($T\uparrow$) means faster.

### Worked example

A protein of radius $r\approx 2$ nm in water ($\eta \approx 10^{-3}$ Pa·s) at 300 K: with $k_BT \approx 4.1\times10^{-21}$ J,

$$D = \frac{4.1\times10^{-21}}{6\pi\times10^{-3}\times2\times10^{-9}} \approx 1.1\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m^2/s},$$

about $0.1\ \mu\mathrm{m^2/ms}$ — roughly ten times slower than a small ion, as expected for a particle ten times larger. Note $D\propto 1/r$, so size matters only linearly, not as volume.

### Why it's true / how it works

This is a **fluctuation–dissipation** relation: the *same* random molecular collisions that *kick* the particle around (driving diffusion, the fluctuation) also *resist* its motion (the viscous drag, the dissipation). Einstein derived $D = k_BT/\gamma$ where $\gamma$ is the drag coefficient; substituting Stokes' $\gamma = 6\pi\eta r$ for a sphere gives the result. The thermal energy $k_BT$ in the numerator is no accident — it is what powers the wandering.

### Where it connects

It sets the $D$ that enters **Fick's laws**, the **random walk**, the **Smoluchowski** diffusion-limited rate, and the **Langevin** equation (where $\gamma$ is the friction). It is the basis for measuring molecular size from diffusion (dynamic light scattering, FRAP, NMR diffusion).

### Watch out

It assumes a **rigid sphere** in a continuum fluid much smaller than the particle — questionable for small molecules, rod-like DNA, or crowded cytoplasm. Real biomolecules are non-spherical and the cell interior is far more viscous and crowded than water, so in-cell $D$ can be several-fold lower than the dilute-water estimate.

### Numbers & nuance

Because $D \propto 1/r$, halving a particle's radius only doubles its diffusion — size matters surprisingly weakly, which is why a 50 kDa protein and a 5 kDa peptide differ in $D$ by only ~2×, not 10×. Temperature and viscosity matter directly: warming water from 20 °C to 37 °C both raises $T$ and lowers $\eta$, speeding diffusion ~40%. Crucially, the intracellular environment is **crowded** (proteins occupy 20–30% of volume) and locally far more viscous than water, so in-cell diffusion coefficients are typically 3–10× below the dilute-water Einstein–Stokes estimate. The relation is also the basis of sizing techniques — dynamic light scattering, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, and pulsed-field-gradient NMR all infer hydrodynamic radius from a measured $D$.

atoms.title: Random walk & mean-square displacement
atoms.summary: Diffusing molecules spread as the square root of time — the microscopic origin of Fick's laws.

depths.eli5: Imagine someone stumbling, each step in a random direction. They drift away from the start, but very inefficiently: to end up twice as far away takes four times as many steps. 'Mean-square displacement' is just the typical squared distance from the start — a fair way to measure spread when the average direction is zero.
depths.core: For unbiased random motion (no preferred direction), the mean-square displacement grows in direct proportion to time: ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt in one dimension (6Dt in three). The typical distance traveled is therefore the square root of that, ∝ √t. This √t scaling is exactly why diffusion is lightning-fast across a few nanometers but hopelessly slow across centimeters — and it's the reason cells that rely on diffusion to feed themselves can't be very large. This random-walk picture is the microscopic origin of Fick's laws.
depths.deep: When ⟨x²⟩ instead grows as t^α with α ≠ 1, you have 'anomalous diffusion': α < 1 (subdiffusion) signals molecular crowding or sticky binding, α > 1 (superdiffusion) signals active transport. Watching single particles inside living cells and measuring α is a rich readout of the crowded cellular interior.

atoms.note: Diffusion time scales as L²/D (distance squared over the diffusion coefficient) — always estimate it before assuming transport across some distance is 'fast'.

quiz.prompt: How does mean-square displacement scale with time for normal diffusion?
quiz.answer: Linearly: ⟨x²⟩ ∝ t (so distance grows as √t).

quiz.prompt: If a molecule needs ~1 ms to diffuse across a 1 µm cell, roughly how long to cross a 10 µm cell?
quiz.answer: ~100 ms — time scales as L²/D, so 10× distance is 100× time.

quiz.prompt: For a 1-D walk of N independent steps of size ±δ (zero mean), derive ⟨x²⟩ and show it leads to ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt. What is the diffusion coefficient in terms of δ and the step time τ?
quiz.answer: x = Σᵢ δᵢ with ⟨δᵢ⟩ = 0 and ⟨δᵢδⱼ⟩ = δ²δ_{ij}; the cross terms vanish, so ⟨x²⟩ = Nδ². With N = t/τ, ⟨x²⟩ = (δ²/τ)t ≡ 2Dt, giving D = δ²/2τ (in 3-D the same argument gives ⟨r²⟩ = 6Dt).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A diffusing molecule does not march in a straight line — it staggers, each step kicked in a random direction by collisions. Such a drunkard's walk does not get far fast: to cover twice the distance it needs *four* times as long. Distance grows like the **square root of time**, which is the microscopic origin of why diffusion is quick over microns but slow over millimetres.

### Precisely

For a one-dimensional random walk, the **mean-square displacement** after time $t$ is

$$\langle x^2\rangle = 2Dt,$$

where $D$ is the diffusion coefficient. The *average* displacement $\langle x\rangle$ is zero (equally likely to go either way), but the *spread* grows. In three dimensions $\langle r^2\rangle = 6Dt$; in $d$ dimensions, $2dDt$. The typical distance travelled therefore scales as $\sqrt{t}$, not $t$.

### Worked example

With $D = 1\ \mu\mathrm{m^2/ms}$ for a small molecule, the time to wander a typical distance $L$ is $t \sim L^2/(2D)$. To cover $1\ \mu$m: $\sim 0.5$ ms. To cover $10\ \mu$m (one cell): $\sim 50$ ms. To cover $100\ \mu$m: $\sim 5$ s. The hundred-fold distance costs a *ten-thousand*-fold time — the brutal $L^2$ penalty.

### Why it's true / how it works

For $N$ independent steps of length $\ell$ and random sign, the displacement is $x=\sum_i \ell_i$. Cross terms average to zero, so $\langle x^2\rangle = N\ell^2$. Since the number of steps is proportional to time, $\langle x^2\rangle \propto t$, and identifying the constant with $2D$ recovers $\langle x^2\rangle = 2Dt$. This is the **same** combinatorics as the **ideal chain**, where steps in *space* replace steps in *time*.

### Where it connects

Averaging this microscopic walk over many particles yields **Fick's laws**; the $D$ here is the Einstein–Stokes $D$. Plotting $\langle x^2\rangle$ vs $t$ is the standard read-out of single-particle tracking; a slope departing from linear flags **anomalous diffusion** (sub- or super-diffusion).

### Watch out

A linear $\langle x^2\rangle\propto t$ holds only for *normal* diffusion. In crowded or trapping environments (cytoplasm, membranes) molecules show **subdiffusion** ($\langle x^2\rangle\propto t^\alpha$, $\alpha<1$). And never confuse the typical distance $\sqrt{\langle x^2\rangle}$ with the mean displacement $\langle x\rangle=0$ — diffusion has no preferred direction, only spread.

### Numbers & nuance

The deep identity is that diffusion in *time* and the ideal polymer coil in *space* are the same combinatorics: $\langle x^2\rangle = 2Dt$ mirrors $\langle R^2\rangle = Nb^2$, with time-steps playing the role of chain segments. A subtle and important point for biology is *dimensionality*: a molecule searching for a target reduces its search drastically by combining 3D diffusion (fast coverage) with 1D sliding along DNA (fine local search) — "facilitated diffusion." And real cellular trajectories often show **anomalous** scaling $\langle x^2\rangle\propto t^\alpha$ with $\alpha<1$ (subdiffusion from crowding and transient binding) or $\alpha>1$ (superdiffusion from active, motor-driven transport) — measuring the exponent $\alpha$ diagnoses the underlying transport mechanism.

atoms.title: The Nernst potential
atoms.summary: The membrane voltage at which an ion's concentration gradient is exactly balanced by the electric field.

depths.eli5: An ion is a charged atom (like sodium or potassium). It naturally wants to drift from where it's crowded to where it's sparse. But because it carries charge, if it piles up on one side it builds a voltage that pushes back. Crank that voltage up to just the right value and the push from crowding exactly cancels the electrical push-back — so on average the ion stops flowing. That exact balancing voltage is the Nernst potential.
depths.core: For an ion the membrane lets through (a 'permeant' ion), there are two forces: a chemical one (from the concentration difference inside vs outside) and an electrical one (from the voltage across the membrane). At the Nernst (equilibrium) potential these two exactly cancel and there's no net flow. Each ion has its own Nernst potential — the 'target' voltage it tries to drag the membrane toward — and these are the foundation of cellular electrophysiology (the study of electrical signals in cells).
depths.deep: When several ions can cross at once, you blend their Nernst potentials weighted by how easily each crosses (its 'permeability') using the Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation to get the cell's resting voltage. But each individual ion's Nernst potential remains the reference point it pulls toward.

atoms.note: At body temperature (310 K), the factor (RT/F)·ln works out to about 61 mV per tenfold (one 'decade') change in concentration ratio, divided by the ion's charge z.

atoms.art_prompt: a membrane with an ion gradient balanced by a voltage, forces canceling

quiz.prompt: What does the Nernst potential represent?
quiz.answer: The membrane voltage at which an ion's chemical gradient is exactly balanced by the electrical force (its equilibrium potential).

quiz.prompt: A 10× outside:inside gradient of a monovalent cation gives roughly what equilibrium potential at body temperature?
quiz.answer: About +61 mV (≈ 61 mV per tenfold ratio for z = +1).

quiz.prompt: Derive the Nernst potential by setting the electrochemical potential of an ion equal on the two sides of the membrane. What is the value per tenfold gradient for a monovalent cation at body temperature?
quiz.answer: Equality of electrochemical potential: RT·ln[in] + zFφ_in = RT·ln[out] + zFφ_out. Solving for E = φ_in − φ_out gives E = (RT/zF)·ln([out]/[in]). For z = +1 at 310 K, RT/F·ln 10 ≈ 61 mV, so each tenfold gradient is worth about 61 mV.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A cell membrane separates two salty solutions with different ion concentrations. An ion wants to diffuse from where it is crowded to where it is sparse — but it carries charge, so moving it builds up a voltage that pushes back. The **Nernst potential** is the exact voltage at which these two pushes — the concentration gradient and the electric field — perfectly cancel, so no net ion flows.

### Precisely

For a single permeant ion, the **equilibrium (Nernst) potential** is

$$E = \frac{RT}{zF}\ln\frac{[\text{ion}]_{\text{out}}}{[\text{ion}]_{\text{in}}},$$

where $R$ is the gas constant, $T$ absolute temperature, $z$ the ion's charge number (e.g. $+1$ for K⁺, $+2$ for Ca²⁺, $-1$ for Cl⁻), and $F$ is **Faraday's constant** (charge per mole of electrons, ~96,485 C/mol). At 37 °C, $RT/F \approx 26.7$ mV, and converting to base-10 logs, $E \approx (61\,\mathrm{mV}/z)\log_{10}([\text{out}]/[\text{in}])$.

### Worked example

For potassium, $[\mathrm{K^+}]_{\text{in}}\approx 140$ mM and $[\mathrm{K^+}]_{\text{out}}\approx 5$ mM, $z=+1$:

$$E_K \approx 61\log_{10}(5/140) = 61\log_{10}(0.036) \approx 61\times(-1.44) \approx -88\ \text{mV}.$$

The strongly negative $E_K$ is why a K⁺-permeable resting membrane sits near $-90$ mV. For Ca²⁺ ($z=+2$, ~$10{,}000\times$ outward gradient), $E_{Ca} \approx +120$ mV — a huge inward driving force.

### Why it's true / how it works

At equilibrium the **electrochemical potential** of the ion is equal on both sides: the chemical part $RT\ln([\text{out}]/[\text{in}])$ exactly balances the electrical part $zFE$. Setting their sum to zero and solving for $E$ gives the Nernst equation. It is the Boltzmann distribution in disguise — ions Boltzmann-distribute across the membrane potential.

### Where it connects

The Nernst potential defines each ion's "battery" $E_i$ in the **Hodgkin–Huxley** circuit, generalizes to many ions at once as the **Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz** equation, sets the driving force in **ion-channel** and **membrane transport**, and reappears for *electrons* as the **redox** Nernst equation.

### Watch out

The Nernst potential is **per ion** — the real resting potential is a permeability-weighted blend of several ions (that's GHK), not any single $E_i$. Also it describes *equilibrium* (zero net flux), not the steady state of a living cell, which constantly leaks and pumps ions and is therefore *not* truly at equilibrium for any ion at once.

### Numbers & nuance

At 37 °C, $RT/F \approx 26.7$ mV and $2.303RT/F \approx 61.5$ mV, so $E \approx (61/z)\log_{10}([\text{out}]/[\text{in}])$ mV. Typical mammalian equilibrium potentials: $E_K\approx -90$ mV, $E_{Na}\approx +60$ mV, $E_{Cl}\approx -65$ mV, $E_{Ca}\approx +120$ mV (Ca²⁺'s huge ~10,000× inward gradient and small denominator $z=2$ give a large positive value). The resting membrane sits near $E_K$ because the resting membrane is mostly K⁺-permeable. Note the *driving force* on an ion is $V_m - E_{\text{ion}}$, not $E_{\text{ion}}$ alone — so even a large $E_{Ca}$ produces current only when channels open and $V_m \neq E_{Ca}$, which is why Ca²⁺ entry is such a sharp, switch-like signal.

atoms.title: Lipid bilayer self-assembly
atoms.summary: Amphiphilic lipids spontaneously form bilayers — the cell's barrier — driven by the hydrophobic effect.

depths.eli5: Lipids are soap-like molecules: one end loves water (the 'head'), the other end is oily and hates water (the 'tails'). Drop a lot of them in water and they spontaneously line up — heads facing out toward the water on both surfaces, oily tails hiding in the middle pointing at each other. The result is a thin double sheet that water can't easily cross: the skin of every cell.
depths.core: Because each lipid has a water-loving (polar) head and water-hating (nonpolar) tails, hiding the tails away from water (the hydrophobic effect) drives them to assemble, all by themselves, into a two-layer sheet — a bilayer. 'Amphiphilic' means having both water-loving and water-hating parts. The sheet is fluid (lipids slide around within it) and self-healing, and it is the structural basis of all cell membranes and of dividing the cell into compartments.
depths.deep: A lipid's overall shape (summarized by its 'packing parameter') decides whether it forms a flat bilayer, a ball-shaped micelle, or other phases. How much energy it costs to bend or fuse a bilayer (see Helfrich elasticity) governs vesicles (tiny membrane bubbles), membrane shaping, and the formation of pores.

atoms.art_prompt: amphiphilic lipids assembling tail-to-tail into a fluid bilayer sheet

quiz.prompt: What drives lipids to form a bilayer?
quiz.answer: The hydrophobic effect — burying the nonpolar tails away from water.

quiz.prompt: Why is a bilayer described as 'self-healing'?
quiz.answer: Exposing tails to water is costly, so the bilayer spontaneously reseals to minimize that exposure.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **lipid** is a molecule with a split personality: a water-loving (**hydrophilic**) head and two water-hating (**hydrophobic**) oily tails — it is **amphiphilic** ("both-loving"). Drop many in water and they cannot satisfy both halves alone. Their solution is to line up into a double sheet — a **bilayer** — tails pointing inward toward each other (hidden from water), heads facing out into the water on both sides. That self-built sheet is the cell's boundary.

### Precisely

A **lipid bilayer** is a two-molecule-thick sheet (~4–5 nm) in which two leaflets of lipids point their hydrophobic tails together and their polar heads toward the surrounding water. It forms spontaneously by the **hydrophobic effect**: hiding the tails from water maximizes the water's entropy. The bilayer is a **two-dimensional fluid** — lipids diffuse rapidly within each leaflet but rarely flip across (slow "flip-flop").

### Worked example

Why a *bilayer* rather than a ball (**micelle**)? The geometry is set by the **packing parameter** $p = v/(a_0 l)$, where $v$ is tail volume, $l$ tail length, and $a_0$ headgroup area. Single-tailed lipids ($p<1/2$) curve into spherical micelles; double-tailed phospholipids ($p\approx 1$, cylindrical shape) pack into flat bilayers. Two tails per head is exactly what tips the geometry from sphere to sheet.

### Why it's true / how it works

Each exposed hydrophobic tail forces surrounding water into an ordered cage (low entropy). Assembling tails into the bilayer interior releases that caged water to the disordered bulk, raising entropy and lowering free energy — the same hydrophobic driving force that folds proteins. No covalent bonds form; the structure is held by the collective, entropy-driven exclusion of water.

### Where it connects

The bilayer is the substrate for the **Nernst/GHK** potentials, **ion channels** and **transporters**, **Hodgkin–Huxley** excitability, and its mechanics are described by the **Helfrich** bending energy. Self-assembly here is the same physics as **micelles** and **condensates**.

### Watch out

Bilayers are **fluid**, not rigid — the old "static sandwich" image is wrong; lipids and proteins diffuse laterally (the fluid-mosaic model). And the bilayer is a barrier to *ions and polar molecules* but quite permeable to small *nonpolar* gases (O₂, CO₂), which dissolve straight through the oily core.

### Numbers & nuance

A bilayer is ~4–5 nm thick with a ~3 nm hydrophobic core; lipids diffuse laterally fast (~1 µm²/s, crossing a bacterium in seconds) but flip between leaflets extremely slowly (hours, unless flippase enzymes help), which lets cells maintain *asymmetric* leaflets. The packing parameter $p=v/(a_0 l)$ predicts morphology: $p<1/3$ → spherical micelles, $1/3<p<1/2$ → cylindrical micelles, $1/2<p<1$ → flexible bilayers/vesicles, $p\approx1$ → planar bilayers, $p>1$ → inverted phases. Two tails per headgroup put phospholipids squarely in the bilayer regime. Bilayers are excellent barriers to ions and polar solutes (permeability for Na⁺ is ~$10^{-14}$ cm/s) but quite permeable to small nonpolar gases — a selectivity that makes channels and transporters necessary for everything charged.

atoms.title: Hodgkin–Huxley & the action potential
atoms.summary: Voltage-gated ion conductances make the membrane an excitable circuit that fires all-or-none spikes.

depths.eli5: A nerve cell's surface is dotted with tiny gates that open and close depending on the voltage across the membrane. When voltage rises past a threshold, sodium gates fling open and the voltage spikes upward; then potassium gates open and bring it back down. That fast up-then-down pulse is a nerve 'spike', and chains of these spikes are how neurons talk.
depths.core: Treat the membrane as an electrical circuit: a capacitor (it stores charge) wired in parallel with several ion-specific 'conductances' (how easily each ion flows). Hodgkin and Huxley wrote equations showing how voltage-dependent sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) conductances — controlled by 'gating variables' that track how open the gates are — generate the action potential: a fast Na⁺ inflow drives the voltage up (depolarization), then a slower K⁺ outflow brings it back down (repolarization). Each ion current pushes the voltage toward that ion's Nernst potential.
depths.deep: This was a quantitative, predictive model fit to careful voltage-clamp measurements (a technique that holds the voltage fixed and reads the resulting current) — a landmark of biophysics. Remarkably, the abstract gating variables foreshadowed the real molecular machinery of voltage-gated ion channels discovered decades later.

resources.label: Wikipedia — Voltage clamp (the data it was fit to)
Wikipedia — Nernst equation (the target each current drives toward)

atoms.art_prompt: a membrane equivalent circuit with Na and K conductance branches producing a spike

quiz.prompt: Which two ion conductances chiefly generate the classic action potential, and what does each do?
quiz.answer: Voltage-gated Na⁺ (fast depolarization) and K⁺ (slower repolarization).

quiz.prompt: Why does each ionic current term have the form g_i(V − E_i)?
quiz.answer: It is Ohm's law with E_i the ion's Nernst potential: the driving force is the deviation of V from equilibrium, scaled by conductance g_i.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A nerve cell's membrane is a tiny battery wrapped in switchable leaks. Normally it sits at a negative voltage. Poke it past a threshold and **voltage-gated** ion channels snap open in a self-reinforcing burst: sodium rushes in, spikes the voltage upward, then potassium channels open and yank it back down. The result is a stereotyped, **all-or-none** electrical pulse — the **action potential** — that travels down the axon.

### Precisely

The membrane is modelled as a capacitor in parallel with voltage-dependent conductances:

$$C\frac{dV}{dt} = -\sum_i g_i(V)\,(V - E_i) + I_{\text{ext}},$$

where $C$ is membrane capacitance, $V$ the voltage, $E_i$ the **Nernst potential** ("battery") of ion $i$, $g_i(V)$ its voltage- and time-dependent **conductance**, and $I_{\text{ext}}$ injected current. Each term $g_i(V)(V-E_i)$ is an ionic current by Ohm's law, with $(V-E_i)$ the driving force. Hodgkin and Huxley fit $g_{\mathrm{Na}}$ and $g_{\mathrm{K}}$ with empirical gating variables $m,h,n$ obeying first-order kinetics.

### Worked example

At rest ($V\approx -70$ mV) channels are mostly shut. A stimulus depolarizes the membrane; near threshold, Na⁺ conductance activates ($m$ rises), Na⁺ current ($E_{\mathrm{Na}}\approx +50$ mV, so inward) depolarizes further, opening *more* Na⁺ channels — **positive feedback** drives the upstroke toward $+40$ mV. Then Na⁺ channels inactivate ($h$ falls) and the slower K⁺ conductance ($n$ rises, $E_K\approx -90$ mV) repolarizes and briefly hyperpolarizes the cell, enforcing a refractory period.

### Why it's true / how it works

The all-or-none spike is a **threshold** phenomenon: below threshold, K⁺ leak wins and the perturbation decays; above it, Na⁺ positive feedback wins and a full spike fires regardless of stimulus size. The shape is set entirely by the voltage dependence and kinetics of the two conductances — a quantitative triumph that earned the 1963 Nobel Prize.

### Where it connects

Each $E_i$ comes from the **Nernst** equation; the resting blend is **GHK**; spatial spread along the axon is the **cable equation**; the underlying single-channel currents are read by **patch clamp**; and the conductance mechanisms are **ion-channel gating**.

### Watch out

$g_i(V)$ is **not** constant — its voltage and time dependence is the whole story; treating channels as fixed resistors loses the excitability. And $m,h,n$ are empirical fits to macroscopic currents, later explained mechanistically by voltage-sensor and inactivation-gate motions seen in single channels.

### Numbers & nuance

Key quantities: membrane capacitance is ~1 µF/cm² (a near-universal constant set by the ~4 nm bilayer acting as a dielectric), resting potential ~$-70$ mV, action-potential peak ~$+40$ mV, and the whole spike lasts ~1–2 ms. The threshold (~$-55$ mV) is the voltage at which inward Na⁺ current just exceeds outward K⁺ current, triggering runaway positive feedback. The gating variables obey $m,h$ (fast Na⁺ activation/inactivation) and $n$ (slower K⁺ activation), each relaxing with voltage-dependent time constants. Tetrodotoxin (blocks Na⁺ channels) and tetraethylammonium (blocks K⁺) let Hodgkin and Huxley dissect the two currents separately — the experimental logic that turned a circuit equation into a quantitative, predictive model of nerve excitation.

atoms.title: Elastic network models (GNM/ENM)
atoms.summary: Model a protein as nodes connected by springs; the soft normal modes predict functional flexibility remarkably well.

depths.eli5: Forget all the chemistry: just pretend a protein is a bunch of balls (one per amino acid) joined by springs wherever two balls sit close together. Now ask where this toy springs-and-balls model naturally wobbles most. Astonishingly, those wobbly spots match the floppy parts of the real protein. Shape and connectivity, not chemical detail, carry most of the flexibility information.
depths.core: The Gaussian Network Model (GNM) connects any two residues closer than a cutoff distance with identical springs, then finds the natural vibration modes by diagonalizing the network's connectivity matrix (the Kirchhoff matrix — a table of which nodes are linked). Despite ignoring all chemical specifics, its low-frequency (soft) modes reproduce experimental flexibility measures like crystallographic B-factors and simulation RMSF (root-mean-square fluctuation — how much each atom jiggles). The takeaway: flexibility is largely set by which residues contact which (the 'contact topology'), not by chemistry.
depths.deep: Because GNM has essentially no free parameters and is computed analytically (from a formula, not trained on data), it cannot secretly exploit similarity to known proteins ('homology leakage'). That makes it a strong, honest baseline that any machine-learning flexibility predictor must genuinely beat to prove it learned real physics.

atoms.note: A recurring lesson in this corpus: simple physics baselines (like GNM) often match or beat machine learning for predicting flexibility.

Wikipedia — B-factor (the flexibility data it predicts)

atoms.art_prompt: a protein reduced to a spring network with soft low-frequency modes highlighted

quiz.prompt: What does a Gaussian Network Model represent the protein as, and what do its soft modes predict?
quiz.answer: Residues as nodes joined by identical springs; the low-frequency modes predict flexibility (B-factors / RMSF).

quiz.prompt: Why is GNM a good 'honest' baseline for flexibility prediction?
quiz.answer: It is analytic and trained on nothing, so it cannot exploit homology/data leakage — any learned model must beat it fairly.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

You don't need every atom and every chemical detail to predict how a protein *flexes*. Replace it with a child's model: put a bead at each residue and connect nearby beads with identical springs. Astonishingly, the soft, large-scale wiggles of this crude spring toy match the real protein's functional motions — hinges, breathing, domain rocking — remarkably well. Shape constrains motion more than chemistry does.

### Precisely

**Elastic network models (ENM)** — including the **Gaussian network model (GNM)** and the **anisotropic network model (ANM)** — represent a folded protein as nodes (one per residue, at the Cα atom) joined by harmonic springs between all node pairs within a cutoff distance. The energy is purely quadratic. The GNM uses a **Kirchhoff connectivity matrix** (which residues contact which); the ANM uses a full $3N\times3N$ Hessian that also predicts the *directions* of motion. **Normal-mode analysis** then diagonalizes that matrix.

### Worked example

For an enzyme that closes over its substrate, build the ANM and diagonalize. The lowest nonzero mode often *is* the open↔closed hinge motion — the eigenvector points the two domains toward each other. Computing this takes seconds, versus microseconds-to-milliseconds of expensive all-atom MD, yet captures the same dominant collective motion because that motion is dictated by the fold's overall shape.

### Why it's true / how it works

The trick rests on **eigenvalues and normal modes**: near a minimum, motion decomposes into independent modes, and the *softest* (smallest-eigenvalue) modes carry the largest-amplitude, lowest-energy collective displacements. Because these soft modes are determined mainly by the *contact topology* (overall shape), the precise spring constants and chemistry barely matter — explaining why a single uniform spring constant works.

### Where it connects

ENM is the practical workhorse built on **eigenvalues & normal modes**; it complements **molecular dynamics** (fast vs detailed), informs flexible fitting of **cryo-EM** maps, and rationalizes allosteric pathways (**MWC/KNF**) as soft-mode communication.

### Watch out

ENM predicts the *shapes and relative softness* of collective motions, **not** absolute timescales, energy barriers, or anything requiring a realistic energy function — it has no chemistry, no solvent, no barriers. It assumes a single well (one minimum), so it cannot describe large unfolding or conformational *transitions*, only small fluctuations about the native state.

### Numbers & nuance

ENMs are astonishingly cheap and robust: a single uniform spring constant and a contact cutoff (~7–15 Å for Cα networks) reproduce experimental crystallographic **B-factors** (per-residue mobility) with correlation coefficients often >0.6, and the lowest one or two modes frequently match the open↔closed motion seen by comparing different crystal forms. The GNM yields only *magnitudes* of fluctuation (isotropic); the ANM adds *directions* via the full $3N\times3N$ Hessian. Because the soft modes depend mostly on the *shape* of the fold, ENMs transfer across homologs and even across resolution — they are routinely used to *flexibly fit* atomic models into low-resolution cryo-EM density, letting a known structure deform realistically into a new conformational map.

atoms.title: Molecular dynamics
atoms.summary: Integrate Newton's equations on a force field to watch biomolecules move atom-by-atom.

depths.eli5: Molecular dynamics is like a physics video game for atoms. At each instant, the computer works out the force on every atom from its neighbors, nudges each one a tiny step accordingly, and then repeats — millions or billions of times. String the frames together and you get a movie of the molecule wiggling and rearranging, atom by atom.
depths.core: MD numerically solves Newton's law of motion, F = ma (force equals mass times acceleration), one tiny timestep at a time, using a clever stepping recipe called the Verlet algorithm. The forces come from an empirical 'force field' — a set of simple rules for the energy of stretched bonds, bent angles, electrostatic attraction/repulsion, and weak van der Waals contacts. The output is a trajectory (a movie) from which thermodynamic and kinetic properties are computed, connecting structure to function in motion.
depths.deep: The central headache is sampling: simulation steps are femtoseconds (10^-15 s) but biologically interesting events can take milliseconds — a billion-billion-fold gap. To reach rare events you need 'enhanced sampling' tricks (umbrella sampling, metadynamics) or Markov state models that stitch many short simulations into the slow picture.

quiz.prompt: What does molecular dynamics integrate, and with what model of the forces?
quiz.answer: Newton's equations of motion (F = ma), using an empirical force field.

quiz.prompt: What is the central limitation of plain MD, and one way around it?
quiz.answer: The timescale/sampling gap (fs steps vs ms events); enhanced sampling or Markov state models help bridge it.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

If you knew the force on every atom in a protein at each instant, you could step them all forward a tiny bit in time, recompute the forces, step again — and watch the molecule move, like a stop-motion movie made from physics. **Molecular dynamics (MD)** does exactly this: it integrates Newton's laws for every atom to produce a trajectory of the biomolecule jiggling, folding, and binding.

### Precisely

MD numerically solves Newton's equation $\mathbf{F}_i = m_i\,\mathbf{a}_i$ for each atom, where forces come from the negative gradient of a **force field** — an empirical potential energy function $U(\mathbf{r})$ summing bond stretches, angle bends, torsions, van der Waals, and electrostatic terms. A symplectic integrator (e.g. **velocity Verlet**) advances positions and velocities by a tiny timestep $\Delta t$ (typically **2 femtoseconds**, $2\times10^{-15}$ s), limited by the fastest vibrations (bond stretches involving hydrogen).

### Worked example

To watch a 100-residue protein in explicit water (tens of thousands of atoms) for $1\ \mu$s requires $10^{-6}/(2\times10^{-15}) = 5\times10^{8}$ timesteps. Each step computes forces on every atom — billions of pairwise interactions per step. This is why microsecond MD historically needed supercomputers or specialized hardware (Anton) or GPUs, and why **enhanced-sampling** and coarse-graining exist.

### Why it's true / how it works

The force field encodes chemistry as classical springs and charges; integrating Newton's equations then *samples* the Boltzmann ensemble (with thermostats/barostats holding $T,P$). Averaging observables over a long trajectory estimates equilibrium properties; watching the time order reveals **kinetics** and pathways that static structures cannot.

### Where it connects

MD generates the trajectories analyzed by **Markov state models** and **normal modes**; its accuracy is set by the force field (now improved by **ML force fields**); rare events it can't reach directly are pried open by **FEP/umbrella sampling/WHAM** and **Metropolis Monte Carlo**; large archives like **mdCATH** make it a data source.

### Watch out

MD's two chronic limits are **timescale** (most biology — folding, large conformational change — is slower than affordable simulation, the *sampling problem*) and **accuracy** (classical force fields are approximations; they cannot break bonds or do quantum chemistry). A pretty trajectory is not proof of convergence — always check that the relevant transitions were sampled enough times to be statistically meaningful.

### Numbers & nuance

Orders of magnitude: timestep 2 fs (set by the fastest bond-stretch vibration, often extended to 4 fs with hydrogen-mass repartitioning); a solvated 50 kDa protein is ~10⁵ atoms; reaching 1 µs needs ~10⁸–10⁹ steps. GPUs and special-purpose hardware (Anton) pushed accessible times from nanoseconds (1990s) to milliseconds, finally overlapping real folding and large conformational changes. The two perennial limits are **sampling** (most biology is still slower than affordable simulation — hence enhanced-sampling and Markov state models) and **force-field accuracy** (classical fixed-charge potentials cannot break bonds or capture polarization — hence ML and polarizable force fields). Thermostats (Langevin, Nosé–Hoover) and barostats hold $T$ and $P$, so a trajectory samples the canonical (NVT) or isothermal-isobaric (NPT) ensemble.

atoms.title: AlphaFold & pLDDT
atoms.summary: Deep learning predicts structure from sequence; pLDDT is its per-residue confidence — often misread as flexibility.

depths.eli5: AlphaFold is an AI that reads a protein's sequence of letters (its amino acids) and guesses the 3D shape it folds into. At each spot it also prints a number saying how confident it is. The trap: people see a low-confidence spot and assume that part of the protein is floppy. But 'the AI is unsure here' is not the same as 'this part actually wiggles'.
depths.core: AlphaFold predicts a protein's 3D structure from its sequence plus a 'multiple-sequence alignment' (a stack of related proteins from other species, which reveals which positions evolved together). It reports pLDDT, a per-residue confidence score from 0 to 100. On average, low-pLDDT regions do tend to be disordered or flexible — but pLDDT is a measure of prediction confidence, not a physical measurement of motion. Whether it can stand in for flexibility was an active 2025 debate.
depths.deep: Treating pLDDT as if it were dynamics is a classic 'observable-mismatch' and data-leakage trap: confidence partly reflects how predictable (e.g. how evolutionarily conserved) a region is, not how much it moves. So an honest flexibility benchmark must compare against an actual physics model (like GNM) and carefully control for homology (similarity to training proteins).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

For decades, predicting a protein's 3D shape from its sequence — the "protein folding problem" — was a grand open challenge. Deep learning cracked it: **AlphaFold** reads a sequence (and its evolutionary relatives) and outputs an accurate 3D structure, often rivaling experiment. Crucially, it also reports how *confident* it is at each position, a per-residue score called **pLDDT**.

### Precisely

**AlphaFold2** is a neural network that takes a query sequence plus a **multiple sequence alignment** (MSA, a stack of evolutionarily related sequences) and predicts atomic coordinates. **pLDDT** (predicted Local Distance Difference Test) is its **per-residue confidence**, scored 0–100: it estimates how well the local geometry around that residue would match a true structure. Roughly: **>90** = very high confidence, **70–90** = confident, **50–70** = low, **<50** = very low.

### Worked example

A globular, well-conserved domain typically scores pLDDT >90 throughout — trust those coordinates. A flexible inter-domain linker or a terminal tail often scores <50. The tempting interpretation is "low pLDDT = flexible region." That is *sometimes* right (intrinsically disordered regions do score low), but pLDDT is fundamentally a **confidence**, not a measured B-factor or flexibility — low score can also mean simply too little evolutionary signal to place that residue.

### Why it's true / how it works

The MSA supplies **coevolution** signal: residues that contact each other in 3D tend to mutate in correlated ways across evolution, so the network infers spatial proximity from sequence covariation. pLDDT is trained to *predict its own accuracy*, so it is high where the evidence (deep alignment, consistent geometry) is strong and low where it is weak — which correlates with, but is not identical to, true disorder.

### Where it connects

It operationalizes **Anfinsen's** sequence→structure principle at scale; complements **ESM** (sequence-only language models); provides starting structures for **MD**, docking, and **ENM**; and pairs with a separate **PAE** (predicted aligned error) map for inter-domain confidence.

### Watch out

The single most common misread is treating pLDDT as a *flexibility* or *B-factor*. It is a **prediction-confidence** metric. Low pLDDT correlates with disorder but can also flag low evolutionary coverage. AlphaFold also predicts one *static* model, not the conformational *ensemble*, and is weakest on mutations' effects, ligands, and multi-state proteins.

### Numbers & nuance

pLDDT bands in practice: >90 (very high — backbone and most side chains trustworthy), 70–90 (confident backbone), 50–70 (low — treat cautiously), <50 (very low — often, but not always, intrinsic disorder). A *separate* metric, the **PAE** (Predicted Aligned Error) matrix, reports confidence in *relative* positions between residues/domains — essential for judging whether two high-pLDDT domains are correctly *oriented* with respect to each other. AlphaFold2's median backbone accuracy at CASP14 reached ~1 Å for well-folded domains, a step change that effectively solved single-domain structure prediction. But it predicts one *static* model from evolutionary signal — it is weakest on mutational effects, ligand-bound states, multiple conformations, and proteins with shallow alignments, where the coevolution signal runs thin.

atoms.title: Protein language models (ESM)
atoms.summary: Transformers trained on millions of sequences learn representations that predict structure, function, and mutation effects.

depths.eli5: Treat each protein as a sentence written in a 20-letter alphabet (the amino acids). Show an AI millions of these 'sentences' and have it play fill-in-the-blank — hide a letter and make it guess. To win the game it has to learn the hidden grammar of proteins, which turns out to be enough to predict structure and to estimate what happens when you change a letter.
depths.core: Just like a text language model, ESM (Evolutionary Scale Modeling) is trained by 'masked-token prediction' — hide an amino acid and predict it — over huge databases of protein sequences (this is 'self-supervised' learning: the data labels itself). The model's internal representations ('embeddings') capture evolutionary and structural signal that's reusable for other tasks. But on some tasks, like predicting flexibility, sequence-only models can lose to simple physics and can secretly rely on similarity to training proteins.
depths.deep: To judge these models honestly you must test on proteins whose folds don't appear in training — e.g. splits that keep whole CATH superfamilies separate. Otherwise the apparent skill is partly memorized homology (recognizing near-copies of training data) rather than transferable biophysics.

atoms.note: A theme across modern biophysics ML: control for homology leakage (test on truly novel folds) or your benchmark will flatter the model and lie to you.

quiz.answer: By masked-token prediction over large databases of protein sequences (self-supervised).
