Wikipedia — Oxidative phosphorylation (its role in respiration)

atoms.art_prompt: a membrane c-ring turbine spun by proton flow, its central stalk rotating inside a three-lobed catalytic head cycling loose-tight-open and ejecting ATP

quiz.prompt: In Boyer's binding-change mechanism, what does rotation of the γ-stalk do to the catalytic sites?
quiz.answer: It cycles each of the three β catalytic sites through loose, tight, and open conformations, so substrate binds (loose), ATP forms (tight), and ATP is released (open) — yielding three ATP per full rotation.

quiz.prompt: ATP synthase is reversible. What does it do when run backward, and what physically determines protons consumed per ATP?
quiz.answer: Run backward it hydrolyzes ATP to pump protons against their gradient. The protons-per-ATP ratio is set by the number of c-subunits in the rotor ring (its mechanical gearing), which varies across organisms.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

ATP synthase is a literal rotary motor — a molecular turbine. Protons flowing down their gradient spin a wheel embedded in the membrane; that wheel is connected to a central shaft that rotates inside a stationary barrel. As the shaft turns, it mechanically deforms three catalytic sites in sequence, squeezing ADP and phosphate together to form ATP. It converts an electrochemical gradient into rotation, and rotation into chemical bonds.

### Precisely

**ATP synthase** is a two-motor machine. The membrane-embedded **F₀** motor lets protons flow down the **proton-motive force**, driving rotation of a ring of c-subunits and the attached central **γ-shaft**. The **F₁** head (three αβ catalytic pairs) is held fixed by a stator; the rotating γ-shaft cyclically forces each catalytic site through three conformations — **open** (releases ATP), **loose** (binds ADP + Pᵢ), and **tight** (forms ATP). This is the **binding-change mechanism**.

### Worked example

If the c-ring has, say, 10 subunits, one full 360° rotation transports ~10 protons and synthesizes 3 ATP (one per αβ pair) — giving an H⁺/ATP ratio of ~3.3. The motor is also **reversible**: run ATP synthase backward (hydrolyzing ATP) and it *pumps* protons, which is how some bacteria use it. Single-molecule experiments have directly *watched* the γ-shaft rotate in discrete steps.

### Why it's true / how it works

Proton flow through F₀ is harnessed by alternating protonation of c-ring sites at the two half-channels, biasing the ring's Brownian rotation in one direction (a rectified-noise motor). The torque on the asymmetric γ-shaft cyclically strains the three F₁ sites; the **tight** conformation makes ATP formation from bound ADP+Pᵢ nearly spontaneous (the hard step is *releasing* ATP, which the rotation drives). Boyer and Walker won the Nobel for this mechanism.

### Where it connects

It is the consumer of the **proton-motive force** from **chemiosmosis** and the **electron transport chain**, a prime example of a **molecular motor** rectifying thermal noise, and of mechanochemical **coupling** between a gradient and bond formation.

### Watch out

The energetically costly step is **not** forming the ATP bond (which is near-equilibrium in the tight site) but **releasing** the product and binding substrates — the rotation pays for those conformational changes. And the machine is fully **reversible**: direction depends on whether the proton gradient or the ATP/ADP ratio dominates, so the same enzyme can make or burn ATP.

### Numbers & nuance

The c-ring stoichiometry (8–15 subunits, species-dependent) fixes the H⁺/ATP ratio: with three catalytic sites per 360° turn, an $n$-subunit ring gives $n/3$ protons per ATP (~3–4 typical). Single-molecule rotation assays directly *watched* the γ-shaft spin in 120° steps (one per ATP), confirming the binding-change mechanism. The enzyme is fully **reversible** — its direction is set by the balance between the proton-motive force and the ATP/ADP·Pᵢ ratio, so it synthesizes ATP when the gradient dominates and *hydrolyzes* ATP to pump protons when it doesn't (some bacteria run it this way to maintain their membrane potential). The energetically expensive step is releasing tightly-bound ATP, which the rotation drives — not forming the bond, which is near-equilibrium in the tight site.

atoms.title: KNF sequential allostery
atoms.summary: The induced-fit alternative to MWC: each ligand binding reshapes its own subunit and, through subunit contacts, changes neighbors' affinities one step at a time.

depths.eli5: Instead of the whole protein flipping at once, each subunit changes shape only when it grabs a ligand, and that change nudges its neighbors to bind better (or worse) — a chain reaction rather than a single switch.
depths.core: The Koshland–Némethy–Filmer model is built on induced fit: a subunit changes conformation only upon binding its ligand, and inter-subunit coupling then alters neighboring sites' affinities. Unlike MWC, KNF allows intermediate hybrid states (some subunits in each conformation) and can produce negative cooperativity, which MWC cannot. Real allosteric proteins often fall between the two limits.
depths.deep: MWC = conformational selection from a pre-existing equilibrium of symmetric states; KNF = induced fit with sequential, asymmetric changes. The distinction maps onto a modern energy-landscape view: both are limits of a fuller ensemble description where ligands reweight a continuum of conformations. Experiments distinguishing them look for the symmetry-breaking intermediates KNF permits and the negative cooperativity MWC forbids.

atoms.note: MWC vs KNF in one line: all-subunits-together 'conformational selection' (MWC, can't be negatively cooperative) vs one-at-a-time 'induced fit' (KNF, can be). Reality usually sits between. ('Induced fit' = the protein reshapes its site in response to binding; 'conformational selection' = the ligand just picks a shape that was already there.)

resources.label: Wikipedia — Allosteric regulation (KNF is one model of it)
Wikipedia — Conformational change (the induced-fit shape change)

atoms.art_prompt: an oligomer binding ligands one subunit at a time, each bound subunit changing shape and tugging its neighbor's affinity, with mixed-conformation intermediates

quiz.prompt: What is the central assumption of the KNF model, and what behavior can it explain that MWC cannot?
quiz.answer: Induced fit: a subunit changes conformation only upon binding ligand, sequentially altering neighbors' affinities. KNF can produce negative cooperativity (and mixed-conformation intermediates), which the concerted MWC model cannot.

quiz.prompt: How would you experimentally distinguish KNF from MWC behavior in an oligomer?
quiz.answer: Look for symmetry-breaking intermediates (subunits in different conformations at partial saturation) and for negative cooperativity — both are allowed by KNF's sequential induced fit but forbidden by MWC's concerted, symmetric switching.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Here is the rival picture to MWC. Instead of all subunits flipping shape together, imagine that binding a ligand reshapes *only the subunit it lands on* — molding that site to fit (an "induced fit"). That local reshaping then nudges the neighbouring subunits through their contacts, changing *their* affinity for the next ligand. Cooperativity spreads subunit by subunit, one handshake at a time, rather than all at once.

### Precisely

The **Koshland–Némethy–Filmer (KNF)** model explains cooperativity by **sequential induced fit**: ligand binding induces a conformational change in *its own* subunit (no pre-existing R/T equilibrium required), and **subunit–subunit interactions** transmit that change to neighbours, altering their binding affinities. Crucially, KNF permits **mixed** conformations (some subunits changed, some not) and can produce **negative** as well as positive cooperativity.

### Worked example

In a four-subunit protein, the first ligand binds an empty subunit and reshapes it; if the induced change is communicated favourably to neighbours, the *second* ligand binds more tightly (positive cooperativity). But if the change makes neighbours bind *less* tightly, you get **negative cooperativity** — a behaviour the symmetric MWC model cannot produce, making negative cooperativity a fingerprint of KNF-like mechanisms.

### Why it's true / how it works

KNF rests on **induced fit**: the ligand actively *reshapes* its site rather than selecting a pre-formed shape. Because conformational changes are passed through physical subunit interfaces step by step, intermediate (mixed) states are allowed, giving KNF more flexibility than MWC's all-or-none concerted switch — at the cost of more parameters.

### Where it connects

KNF is the **sequential / induced-fit** counterpart to **MWC**'s **concerted / conformational-selection** model; both explain the cooperativity summarized empirically by the **Hill** equation. Real proteins (haemoglobin included) often lie *between* the two extremes, and the debate maps onto the modern **conformational selection vs induced fit** and **energy-landscape** framework.

### Watch out

KNF and MWC are **limiting idealizations**, not mutually exclusive truths — most allosteric proteins show features of both. The clean test that favours KNF is **negative cooperativity**, which pure symmetric MWC forbids; seeing it tells you the mechanism is at least partly sequential/induced-fit.

### Numbers & nuance

The clean discriminator between the two allostery models is **negative cooperativity**: KNF's sequential, induced-fit mechanism permits *mixed* conformational states and can make later ligands bind *weaker* — something pure symmetric MWC forbids. So observing negative cooperativity is positive evidence for a KNF-like (or hybrid) mechanism. The cost of KNF's flexibility is more parameters (per-step interaction energies) than MWC's three. Real proteins, haemoglobin included, lie on a continuum between the concerted (MWC, conformational selection) and sequential (KNF, induced fit) extremes, and the modern ensemble/energy-landscape view subsumes both: allostery is a *redistribution of conformational populations*, whether ligand selects a pre-existing state (MWC-like) or actively reshapes one and propagates the change (KNF-like).

atoms.title: pKa shifts in proteins
atoms.summary: A protein's electrostatic environment shifts the acid–base equilibria of ionizable residues away from their solution values — the physical basis of enzyme catalysis and pH sensing.

depths.eli5: An amino acid's willingness to hold or release a proton depends on its neighbors. Bury it near a positive charge and it lets go more easily; near a negative charge it clings tighter. The protein tunes these to do chemistry.
depths.core: Each ionizable group has an intrinsic solution pKa, but inside a protein its effective pKa is shifted by the local electrostatics: desolvation (burial in low dielectric disfavors charge, raising acidic pKa / lowering basic pKa), nearby fixed charges, and hydrogen bonds. The shift is ΔpKa = ΔΔG/(2.303·RT), where ΔΔG is the electrostatic free-energy change of the charged versus neutral form. Continuum electrostatics (Poisson–Boltzmann) is the standard tool to compute it.
depths.deep: Catalysis often exploits dramatic shifts: an active-site aspartate or histidine may be shifted by several pH units so it is protonated or deprotonated at physiological pH precisely when needed for proton shuttling. Buried, electrostatically frustrated groups can shift pKa by 4–5 units; networks of coupled ionizable residues give pH-dependent conformational switches (e.g. in viral fusion and proton pumps). Measuring these shifts (NMR titration) directly probes the electrostatic model and is a stringent test of PB-based predictions.

atoms.note: A pKa shift is electrostatic free energy in disguise: ΔpKa = ΔΔG/(2.303·RT). Enzymes engineer these shifts to put a proton on (or off) a key group exactly where catalysis needs it. ('pKa' is the pH at which an acidic/basic group is half-protonated — lower pKa means it gives up its proton more readily; 'ionizable' = able to gain or lose a proton.)

resources.label: Wikipedia — Poisson–Boltzmann equation (the tool to compute shifts)
Wikipedia — Enzyme catalysis (where shifts are exploited)

atoms.art_prompt: an ionizable side chain buried near fixed charges in a protein, its titration curve shifted left or right from the solution value, dielectric boundary drawn

quiz.prompt: Name three factors inside a protein that shift an ionizable residue's pKa from its solution value.
quiz.answer: Desolvation (burial in a low-dielectric interior), nearby fixed charges (favorable or unfavorable), and hydrogen bonding to the ionizable group. All are electrostatic contributions to the charged-vs-neutral free energy.

quiz.prompt: Relate a residue's pKa shift to an electrostatic free-energy change.
quiz.answer: ΔpKa = ΔΔG_elec/(2.303·RT), where ΔΔG_elec is the change in free energy of forming the charged state inside the protein relative to in solution. A positive electrostatic penalty for the charge of an acid raises its pKa; stabilizing it lowers the pKa.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Whether an amino acid's chemical group holds onto its proton (stays protonated) or lets it go depends on the pH — and on its *surroundings*. A charged group placed in the greasy, low-dielectric interior of a protein, or next to another charge, behaves very differently from the same group floating free in water. Proteins exploit these shifts to make a residue grab or release protons exactly when catalysis demands — tuning their own acid–base chemistry.

### Precisely

The **pKa** of an ionizable group is the pH at which it is half-protonated; below pKa it is mostly protonated, above it mostly deprotonated (from the **Henderson–Hasselbalch** relation). Inside a protein, the local electrostatic environment **shifts** each residue's pKa away from its standard solution value. Burying a charge in a low-dielectric pocket, or placing it near like/unlike charges, can shift pKa by several units. The microscopic origin is the free-energy cost/benefit of the charged vs neutral form in that environment.

### Worked example

A glutamate (solution pKa ~4.2) buried in a hydrophobic active site, far from compensating charge, finds its charged (deprotonated) form destabilized — so it clings to its proton, and its pKa rises by several units. At physiological pH ~7 it can therefore stay *protonated* when it "shouldn't," letting it act as a proton donor in catalysis. The reverse — a lysine with an abnormally *low* pKa acting as a base — occurs in some enzymes for the opposite reason.

### Why it's true / how it works

Charging a group costs free energy that depends on the surrounding **dielectric** (water shields charge well; protein interior poorly) and on nearby charges (the **Poisson–Boltzmann** electrostatics). A larger penalty for the charged state pushes the equilibrium toward neutral, *raising* the pKa of acids (and lowering it for bases). These shifts are computed with PB/continuum-electrostatics methods.

### Where it connects

It is electrostatics (**Debye/Poisson–Boltzmann**) applied to titration, underlies **enzyme catalysis** (general acid/base residues), pH sensing, and the protonation states feeding **MD** and **redox** chemistry.

### Watch out

Standard solution pKa values are *not* reliable inside a protein — assuming them is a classic error that misassigns protonation states and ruins mechanism analysis and simulations. pKa is also **coupled**: nearby ionizable groups influence each other, so they often must be solved together, not one at a time.

### Numbers & nuance

Solution reference pKa values: Asp ~3.7, Glu ~4.2, His ~6.0, Cys ~8.3, Tyr ~10, Lys ~10.5, Arg ~12.5. Inside a protein these can shift by several units — burying an acid's charged (deprotonated) form in a low-dielectric pocket *raises* its pKa (it clings to its proton), while burying a base's charged form *lowers* its pKa; nearby charges add Coulombic shifts. Enzymes exploit this to position a residue that is a good proton donor or acceptor at physiological pH 7 — the heart of acid–base catalysis. pKa values are **coupled** (neighbouring ionizable groups influence each other), so they are computed together via Poisson–Boltzmann/continuum electrostatics, and naively assuming solution values inside a protein is a classic, mechanism-wrecking error.

atoms.title: Ion channel gating & selectivity
atoms.summary: Channels open and close (gate) in response to voltage, ligands, or force, and a selectivity filter passes the right ion at near-diffusion-limited rates — the molecular basis of excitability.

depths.eli5: Ion channels are doors in the membrane that snap open and shut, and they are picky about which ion they let through. A voltage-sensing part feels the membrane's charge and pulls the door open.
depths.core: Gating is a conformational equilibrium between closed and open states biased by a stimulus. For voltage-gated channels, charged S4 helices (gating charges) move in the field, so the open probability follows a Boltzmann function of voltage, P_open = 1/(1 + e^(−zF(V−V₁/₂)/RT)), where z is the effective gating charge. Selectivity comes from a filter that coordinates the dehydrated ion with backbone carbonyls mimicking its hydration shell — K⁺ channels fit K⁺ but not the smaller Na⁺, conducting at ~10⁷–10⁸ ions/s near the diffusion limit.
depths.deep: The single-channel current is stochastic — it blinks open and closed (resolved by patch clamp) — and the macroscopic conductance g_i(V) in Hodgkin–Huxley is the ensemble average of these gating probabilities. Selectivity is a thermodynamic balance: the energetic cost of stripping the ion's hydration shell must be repaid by the filter's coordination, a 'snug-fit' tuned to the target ion's radius. Inactivation (a separate gate) and modulation by lipids and second messengers make channels rich computational elements, not simple resistors.

atoms.note: The Boltzmann voltage-dependence of the open probability is what produces the conductance g(V) in Hodgkin–Huxley; 'selectivity' is the filter repaying an ion's cost of shedding its water shell by coordinating it exactly. ('Gating' = opening/closing; 'selectivity filter' = the narrow stretch that admits only the right ion; 'dehydration' = stripping off the ion's surrounding water.)

atoms.art_prompt: a voltage-gated channel with charged S4 helices moving in the membrane field, a selectivity filter coordinating a dehydrated K⁺ ion, a sigmoidal open-probability-vs-voltage curve

quiz.prompt: Why does the open probability of a voltage-gated channel follow a Boltzmann (sigmoidal) function of membrane voltage?
quiz.answer: Gating charges (e.g. the S4 helix) move within the membrane electric field, so the open-vs-closed free-energy difference is linear in voltage; the equilibrium population of the open state is then a Boltzmann function of that voltage-dependent energy.

quiz.prompt: How can a K⁺ channel conduct K⁺ but exclude the smaller Na⁺ ion?
quiz.answer: The selectivity filter's carbonyl oxygens are spaced to coordinate a dehydrated K⁺ exactly as water would, repaying its dehydration cost; the smaller Na⁺ does not fit snugly enough for the filter to compensate its larger dehydration penalty, so it is excluded — a 'snug-fit' thermodynamic discrimination.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

An ion channel is a protein pore that lets specific ions cross the membrane — but it is not a passive hole. It has a **gate** that opens and closes in response to signals (voltage, a bound molecule, or membrane stretch), and a **selectivity filter** that admits the *right* ion while rejecting others, all while passing ions almost as fast as they can diffuse. This combination of fast, selective, *switchable* permeation is the molecular basis of nerve and muscle excitability.

### Precisely

**Gating** is the conformational switching of a channel between non-conducting (closed/inactivated) and conducting (open) states, triggered by **voltage** (a charged voltage-sensor moves in the field), **ligand** binding, or mechanical **force**. The **selectivity filter** is a narrow stretch of pore lined with precisely spaced carbonyl oxygens that mimic the ion's hydration shell — it strips water from the favoured ion and coordinates it, so passing the right ion is energetically cheap and the wrong one costly. Conduction approaches the **diffusion limit** (~10⁶–10⁸ ions/s).

### Worked example

The potassium channel selectivity filter selects K⁺ over the *smaller* Na⁺ — counterintuitively. The filter's backbone oxygens are positioned to replace K⁺'s water shell perfectly, so dehydrating and re-coordinating K⁺ is nearly cost-free; Na⁺ is too small to contact all the oxygens, so shedding its tightly-held water shell is *not* repaid, and it is rejected. Selectivity comes from a precise geometric fit, not just pore size.

### Why it's true / how it works

Gating is a Boltzmann-weighted equilibrium between conformations, biased by voltage (the gating charge times field), ligand binding energy, or membrane tension — so the open probability is a sigmoidal function of the stimulus. Selectivity is thermodynamic: the filter lowers the free-energy barrier for the favoured ion's dehydration-and-permeation pathway relative to competitors.

### Where it connects

It is the molecular machinery behind **Hodgkin–Huxley** conductances $g_i(V)$, the **Nernst/GHK** driving forces, **patch-clamp** single-channel records, and a special case of **membrane transport**; selectivity rests on **Debye**-scale electrostatics and dehydration energetics.

### Watch out

Selectivity is **not** simple size-sieving (the channel selects the *larger* K⁺ over Na⁺) — it is about how well the filter *replaces* each ion's hydration shell. And "closed" and "inactivated" are distinct non-conducting states: inactivation (a separate, slower gate) is what enforces the refractory period in neurons.

### Numbers & nuance

Single channels conduct ~$10^6$–$10^8$ ions/s — near the diffusion limit — yet remain exquisitely selective (the K⁺ channel discriminates K⁺ over the *smaller* Na⁺ by ~1000:1). Selectivity is achieved not by size-sieving but by how perfectly the filter's backbone carbonyl oxygens *replace* the favoured ion's hydration shell: K⁺ fits the geometry so dehydration is repaid, Na⁺ is too small to contact all oxygens so its tightly-held water is not repaid, and it is excluded. Gating is a Boltzmann-weighted switch — open probability is a sigmoidal function of voltage (via the gating-charge movement), ligand concentration, or membrane tension. Distinct non-conducting states (closed vs **inactivated**) matter physiologically: inactivation enforces the neuronal refractory period and sets firing limits.

atoms.title: Membrane transport: pumps, channels & cotransporters
atoms.summary: Cells move solutes across membranes either downhill (passive, through channels) or uphill (active, powered by ATP or a coupled ion gradient) — the bookkeeping of cellular energetics.

depths.eli5: Some doors just let things slide downhill across the membrane. Other machines spend energy to push things uphill — either by burning ATP directly, or by letting one ion fall downhill to drag another one up.
depths.core: Passive transport (channels, facilitated carriers) moves a solute down its electrochemical gradient; the driving force is the difference between membrane voltage and the solute's Nernst potential. Active transport moves solutes uphill, against the gradient. Primary active transport hydrolyzes ATP (e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP). Secondary active transport (cotransport) couples an uphill solute to a downhill ion: symporters move both the same way, antiporters opposite — the energy comes from the ion gradient a primary pump created.
depths.deep: The free energy to move a charged solute is ΔG = RT·ln([S]_in/[S]_out) + zF·Δψ — chemical plus electrical work. Secondary transport is the cell 'spending' the Na⁺ (or H⁺) gradient like a battery the ATP-driven pump charged, which is why the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase consumes a large fraction of cellular ATP: it maintains the gradient that powers nutrient uptake, pH regulation, and volume control. Transporters cycle through alternating-access conformations (outward-open ↔ inward-open), a slow turnover (10²–10³/s) versus a channel's 10⁷–10⁸/s — the speed/control tradeoff between gated pores and conformational carriers.

atoms.note: Pumps charge the battery (primary, ATP-driven), cotransporters spend it (secondary, gradient-driven). The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase's gradient is the cell's universal secondary power source. ('Passive' = moves downhill on its own; 'active' = needs energy to push uphill; a 'symporter' carries two things the same way, an 'antiporter' opposite ways.)

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between primary and secondary active transport?
quiz.answer: Primary active transport uses a direct energy source (usually ATP hydrolysis) to move a solute uphill; secondary active transport (cotransport) couples the uphill movement of one solute to the downhill movement of an ion (e.g. Na⁺ or H⁺) whose gradient was established by a primary pump.

quiz.prompt: Write the free energy to move one mole of a charged solute across a membrane and identify the two contributions.
quiz.answer: ΔG = RT·ln([S]_in/[S]_out) + zFΔψ: a chemical (concentration) term and an electrical (voltage) term. Transport is passive if this is negative for the move and active (needs energy input) if positive.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Cells must move solutes — ions, sugars, amino acids — across their oily membrane barrier. Some solutes ride **downhill** along their gradient (from high to low concentration), which is free and only needs an open path. Others must be forced **uphill**, against their gradient, which costs energy — paid either directly with ATP or by coupling to another ion that *is* flowing downhill. Sorting transport into "downhill, free" versus "uphill, powered" is the basic bookkeeping of cellular energetics.

### Precisely

- **Passive transport** moves solute *down* its electrochemical gradient with no energy input, through **channels** (open pores) or **facilitated carriers**. The driving force is the **Nernst/GHK** electrochemical potential difference.
- **Primary active transport** moves solute *up* its gradient using direct ATP hydrolysis — e.g. the **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase** pump.
- **Secondary active transport** (cotransport) moves one solute uphill by coupling it to another ion flowing downhill: **symporters** (same direction) and **antiporters** (opposite directions).

### Worked example

The **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase** spends one ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per cycle — both uphill — building the Na⁺ gradient. That stored Na⁺ gradient then powers **secondary** transport: the SGLT glucose symporter lets Na⁺ flow back in *downhill* and drags a glucose molecule *uphill* along for the ride. So one primary pump (ATP-driven) funds many secondary uphill transports — an energy economy.

### Why it's true / how it works

The free-energy change for moving an ion is its electrochemical potential difference, $\Delta\mu = RT\ln([\text{in}]/[\text{out}]) + zF\Delta\psi$. Passive transport runs when $\Delta\mu<0$ (downhill). Active transport couples an *unfavourable* $\Delta\mu>0$ to a *favourable* energy source (ATP hydrolysis, or another ion's downhill $\Delta\mu$) so the *sum* is negative and the cycle proceeds.

### Where it connects

It rests on the **Nernst/GHK** potentials, the gradients built by **chemiosmosis** and **ATP synthase**, the gating/selectivity of **ion channels**, and supplies the ionic conditions for **Hodgkin–Huxley** excitability.

### Watch out

Don't confuse **channels** (passive, downhill, fast, gated pores) with **pumps** (active, uphill, ATP-powered, slow). And "active" is defined by *direction relative to the gradient*, not by speed: a transporter is active only if it moves solute *against* its electrochemical gradient by spending energy.

### Numbers & nuance

The energetic bookkeeping uses the electrochemical potential $\Delta\mu = RT\ln([\text{in}]/[\text{out}]) + zF\Delta\psi$: transport is passive (spontaneous) when $\Delta\mu<0$ and requires energy when $\Delta\mu>0$. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP) is the master **primary** pump, and the Na⁺ gradient it builds is then spent by countless **secondary** transporters (SGLT glucose symport, Na⁺/Ca²⁺ antiport) — one ATP-funded pump bankrolls many uphill movements. Throughput hierarchy: channels are fastest (~$10^6$–$10^8$ ions/s, passive), then carriers/cotransporters (~$10^2$–$10^4$/s), then primary pumps (slowest, ~$10^2$/s) because each ATP-driven cycle involves large conformational changes. "Active" is defined by direction against the gradient, not by speed.

atoms.title: Signal transduction biophysics
atoms.summary: Cells convert extracellular ligand binding into intracellular responses through cascades whose biophysics sets sensitivity, gain, noise filtering, and switch-like decisions.

depths.eli5: A signal arrives outside the cell as a molecule docking onto a receptor. The cell then relays and amplifies that message through a chain of molecular switches, deciding whether to act and how strongly.
depths.core: A receptor binds ligand with a K_d that sets the concentration range it detects. Downstream, enzymatic cascades (e.g. kinase phosphorylation) amplify: one active receptor can activate many G-proteins, each producing many second messengers. Ultrasensitivity — a sharp, switch-like input/output relation (effective Hill coefficient ≫ 1) — arises from multistep phosphorylation, zero-order kinetics (Goldbeter–Koshland), or molecular titration, letting cells make near-digital decisions from graded inputs.
depths.deep: Sensitivity is bounded by physics: receptor occupancy fluctuates (shot noise from finite ligand counts), so the Berg–Purcell limit sets how precisely concentration can be measured given diffusion and integration time. Feedback loops add dynamics — negative feedback gives adaptation (the system returns to baseline despite sustained input, as in bacterial chemotaxis) and oscillations; positive feedback gives bistability and memory. Spatial gradients of second messengers, set by a balance of production and degradation/diffusion (a length scale √(D/k)), localize responses within the cell.

atoms.note: Three recurring design moves: amplification (one input triggers many outputs), ultrasensitivity (a gradual input becomes a sharp on/off output), and feedback (adaptation, bistability, oscillation). All are quantifiable from binding strengths and reaction rates. ('Second messenger' = a small molecule made inside the cell to relay a signal; 'kinase' = an enzyme that switches targets on/off by attaching a phosphate.)

resources.label: Wikipedia — Second messenger system (the relay molecules)

atoms.art_prompt: a receptor binding a ligand, a branching kinase cascade amplifying the signal, a steep ultrasensitive input-output curve, and a feedback loop returning the system to baseline

quiz.prompt: What is ultrasensitivity in a signaling pathway, and name one mechanism that produces it.
quiz.answer: A sharp, switch-like input/output relationship (effective Hill coefficient much greater than 1), turning a graded signal into a near-digital response. Mechanisms include multistep phosphorylation, zero-order ultrasensitivity (Goldbeter–Koshland), and molecular titration.

quiz.prompt: What does negative feedback contribute to a signaling response, with a biological example?
quiz.answer: It produces adaptation — the response returns toward baseline despite a sustained stimulus (and can generate oscillations). Bacterial chemotaxis is the classic example: the cell adapts to a constant attractant level so it can keep sensing further changes.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A cell must convert an outside message — a hormone or growth factor binding a surface receptor — into an inside decision: divide, move, secrete. The relay that carries the message inward is a **signalling cascade**. Its biophysics determines how *sensitive* the cell is (does a faint signal register?), how much it *amplifies*, how it *filters noise*, and whether it responds gradually or as a sharp **switch**. The same molecular logic appears across biology.

### Precisely

**Signal transduction** is the conversion of extracellular ligand binding into intracellular responses through chains of molecular events — receptor activation, second messengers, kinase cascades. Key biophysical features: **amplification** (one active enzyme activates many substrates, multiplying the signal), **ultrasensitivity** (a switch-like, sigmoidal input–output relation), **adaptation** (returning to baseline despite a sustained stimulus), and **noise filtering** (averaging out random fluctuations). These emerge from the network's kinetics and feedback, not any single molecule.

### Worked example

A kinase cascade (kinase A activates B activates C) can be **ultrasensitive**: if each step operates near saturation, a small fractional change in input produces a steep, switch-like change in output — effectively a high apparent **Hill** coefficient — even though each enzyme is non-cooperative. **Zero-order ultrasensitivity** (Goldbeter–Koshland) arises when opposing kinase and phosphatase both run near saturation, sharpening a graded input into a near-digital decision (e.g. all-or-none cell-cycle commitment).

### Why it's true / how it works

Sensitivity, gain, and switch behaviour follow from the **mass-action kinetics** of binding (**K_d**) and enzyme saturation (**Michaelis–Menten**), combined with **feedback** loops. Positive feedback creates bistability and memory; negative feedback creates adaptation and oscillations; cascades multiply small effects (amplification). Noise is filtered by time-averaging when downstream steps are slower than the fluctuations.

### Where it connects

It is built from **binding (K_d)**, **Michaelis–Menten** enzyme kinetics, **cooperativity/Hill** ultrasensitivity, and **membrane** receptors and channels; its spatial versions connect to **reaction–diffusion** patterning.

### Watch out

Switch-like behaviour does **not** require cooperative binding — cascades and zero-order effects can manufacture ultrasensitivity from non-cooperative parts, so a steep dose–response is *not* proof of allostery. And amplification cuts both ways: it boosts signal *and* noise unless the network actively filters.

### Numbers & nuance

The biophysics turns analog inputs into reliable decisions through a few recurring motifs: **amplification** (one ligand-bound receptor activates many G-proteins or kinases, each acting on many substrates — gains of $10^3$–$10^6$), **ultrasensitivity** (cascades and zero-order Goldbeter–Koshland effects manufacture switch-like, high-apparent-Hill responses from non-cooperative parts), **adaptation** (negative feedback returns output to baseline despite sustained input, enabling fold-change detection), and **noise filtering** (slow downstream steps time-average fast fluctuations). Positive feedback adds **bistability** and memory (committed cell-fate decisions); negative feedback can generate **oscillations** (circadian, calcium, NF-κB). Importantly, a steep dose–response is *not* proof of cooperative binding — network structure alone can produce it, so mechanism must be inferred from the components, not the curve shape.

atoms.title: Molecular motors: myosin & kinesin
atoms.summary: Motor proteins convert chemical energy from ATP hydrolysis into directed mechanical motion along cytoskeletal tracks by rectifying thermal noise through a tightly coupled mechanochemical cycle.

depths.eli5: Tiny protein machines walk along molecular tracks inside the cell, carrying cargo. Each step is powered by burning one ATP, and they walk in one direction even though they are constantly jostled by heat.
depths.core: Myosin (on actin) and kinesin (on microtubules) cycle through ATP binding, hydrolysis, and product release, each step gated to a mechanical change. Kinesin walks hand-over-hand in 8 nm steps toward the microtubule plus-end, tightly coupling roughly one ATP per step. The motor doesn't push against thermal motion so much as rectify it: nucleotide state changes bias which conformations and binding states are accessible, ratcheting net displacement in one direction (a Brownian ratchet / power-stroke hybrid).
depths.deep: A motor cannot beat the second law: the free energy of ATP hydrolysis (~20 k_BT under cellular conditions) sets the maximum work per cycle, and the stall force (where the motor stops, ~5–7 pN for kinesin) times the step length must stay below it. Single-molecule optical-trap experiments resolve individual steps, dwell-time distributions (revealing hidden substeps), and the force–velocity relation. Processivity (steps before detaching) requires coordinating two heads so at least one stays bound — the gating that turns a one-shot power stroke into a long walk.

atoms.note: Motors steer thermal noise, they don't defy it: ATP's ~20 k_BT caps the work per step, so stall force × step length must stay under that budget. Tight chemical-to-mechanical coupling (about one ATP burned per step) is the core design principle. ('Rectify' = turn random back-and-forth jiggling into net one-way motion, like a ratchet; 'stall force' = the load at which the motor stops.)

resources.label: Wikipedia — Optical tweezers (how single steps are measured)

atoms.art_prompt: a two-headed kinesin walking hand-over-hand in 8 nm steps along a microtubule, an optical trap measuring its stepwise displacement and stall force, ATP turnover annotated per step

quiz.prompt: How does a molecular motor like kinesin achieve directed motion despite constant thermal buffeting?
quiz.answer: It rectifies thermal motion: ATP binding, hydrolysis, and product release gate conformational and binding-state changes that bias the motor's diffusion in one direction, so net displacement is directional even though individual fluctuations are random. The chemical cycle is tightly coupled to the mechanical step (~1 ATP per 8 nm step).

quiz.prompt: Kinesin takes 8 nm steps and stalls at about 6 pN. Roughly what work does it do per step at stall, and how does that compare to ATP's energy?
quiz.answer: Work ≈ force × distance = 6 pN × 8 nm ≈ 48 pN·nm ≈ 12 k_BT. ATP hydrolysis supplies ~20 k_BT per cycle, so the motor operates below its energy budget (≈60% efficiency at stall), consistent with the second law.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Motor proteins are nanoscale engines that walk along cellular tracks, hauling cargo, contracting muscle, and separating chromosomes. They burn ATP for fuel — but at their tiny scale they are battered by constant thermal jostling far stronger than the forces they generate. The clever trick is not to fight the noise but to **rectify** it: use ATP's chemical energy to bias random thermal motion so the motor steps *forward* far more often than backward, turning chaos into directed motion.

### Precisely

**Molecular motors** like **myosin** (on actin filaments) and **kinesin** (on microtubules) convert the chemical energy of **ATP hydrolysis** into directed mechanical work along a polar cytoskeletal **track**. Each runs a tightly **coupled mechanochemical cycle**: ATP binding, hydrolysis, and product release are mechanically linked to conformational changes (a "**power stroke**" or biased stepping) that advance the motor by a fixed step (~8 nm for kinesin per ATP) toward one end of the track. Tight coupling means roughly one step per ATP.

### Worked example

Kinesin "walks" hand-over-hand: while one head is bound to the microtubule, ATP binding and hydrolysis swing the trailing head forward by ~16 nm (an 8 nm net displacement of the motor) to the next binding site, then the cycle repeats — processively taking many steps before detaching. **Optical-tweezer** experiments measure its ~5–7 pN stall force and resolve the discrete 8 nm steps directly, confirming the one-ATP-per-step coupling.

### Why it's true / how it works

At thermal equilibrium, no machine can do net work (the second law). ATP hydrolysis pushes the motor *out* of equilibrium: by making certain transitions (e.g. forward binding) far more probable than their reverse, the free energy of hydrolysis **rectifies** the otherwise-symmetric thermal motion. The polar track provides the asymmetry (a ratchet direction); the tight chemomechanical coupling ensures the released energy is spent on stepping, not wasted.

### Where it connects

Motors are the mechanical cousins of **ATP synthase** (a rotary motor), are studied by **optical/magnetic tweezers** and single-molecule methods, operate in the **overdamped Langevin** regime (noise-dominated), and power muscle, transport, and cell division.

### Watch out

The power-stroke vs **Brownian ratchet** distinction is subtle — both rectify motion using ATP; the difference is whether the conformational change directly pushes (power stroke) or merely biases diffusion (ratchet), and real motors blend both. The key conceptual error is imagining motors as deterministic engines: at the nanoscale they *exploit* thermal noise rather than overpowering it.

### Numbers & nuance

Concrete numbers: kinesin takes 8 nm steps (one per ATP) along microtubules, moves ~1 µm/s, and stalls at ~5–7 pN; muscle myosin makes ~5–10 nm power strokes generating a few pN; ATP hydrolysis supplies ~20 $k_BT$ (~50 kJ/mol) per cycle, far exceeding the ~few-$k_BT$ work per step, so the cycle is comfortably driven out of equilibrium. The deep principle is that no machine can do net work *at* equilibrium (second law); ATP hydrolysis breaks detailed balance, making forward transitions far more probable than reverse, so the motor **rectifies** thermal noise rather than overpowering it. The polar track sets the direction; tight chemomechanical coupling (~one step per ATP) ensures the hydrolysis energy is spent on motion, not dissipated.

atoms.title: Entropic elasticity of polymer chains
atoms.summary: Stretching a flexible polymer costs free energy not by straining bonds but by reducing the number of available conformations — the restoring force is purely entropic and grows with temperature.

depths.eli5: A floppy molecule resists being pulled straight the way a crumpled chain resists being uncrumpled: there are far fewer ways to be straight than to be tangled, so the chain pulls back toward its messy, high-count state. Heat it and it pulls back harder.
depths.core: An ideal chain has a Gaussian distribution of end-to-end vectors, so stretching it to extension x reduces conformational entropy by ΔS ∝ −x². The free-energy cost F = −TΔS gives a Hookean restoring force f = (3k_BT/Nb²)·x at small extension — a spring whose stiffness rises with temperature, the signature of an entropic (not enthalpic) spring. There is no bond stretching; the resistance is purely statistical.
depths.deep: At large extension the Gaussian model fails and the force diverges as the chain runs out of slack; the worm-like chain interpolation f·l_p/k_BT = x/L − ¼ + 1/[4(1−x/L)²] captures this and fits single-molecule force–extension curves of DNA superbly. Entropic elasticity is why rubber warms when stretched and contracts when heated, and it underlies the mechanics of titin, the nuclear pore mesh, and disordered protein linkers acting as molecular springs.

atoms.note: Stiffness ∝ k_BT is the giveaway: an entropic spring gets STIFFER when heated, the opposite of a normal bond spring. This is exactly what single-molecule pulling experiments measure. ('Entropic' = the restoring force comes from a loss of arrangements, not from straining any bonds; an 'ideal chain' is the random-coil baseline this builds on.)

resources.label: Wikipedia — Entropy (the source of the force)
LibreTexts Chemistry — Physical & Theoretical Chemistry texts

atoms.art_prompt: a coiled chain being pulled taut, the cloud of accessible conformations shrinking as extension grows, a force-extension curve rising then diverging near full extension

quiz.prompt: Why is the restoring force of a stretched flexible polymer called entropic, and how does its stiffness depend on temperature?
quiz.answer: Stretching reduces the number of available chain conformations (lowers entropy) without straining any bonds, so the restoring force comes from the free-energy cost −TΔS. Its stiffness is proportional to k_BT, so the chain gets stiffer as temperature rises — the hallmark of an entropic spring.

quiz.prompt: From the Gaussian end-to-end distribution, sketch why the small-extension force is linear in x.
quiz.answer: The probability of end-to-end vector x is P(x) ∝ exp(−3x²/2Nb²), so the entropy S = k_B·ln P gives free energy F = −TS ∝ (3k_BT/2Nb²)x². The force is f = ∂F/∂x = (3k_BT/Nb²)x — Hookean (linear in x) at small extension.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Stretch a rubber band and it pulls back — but, surprisingly, not because you are straining its chemical bonds. You are pulling its tangled polymer chains *straighter*, and a straight chain has far fewer ways to be arranged than a coiled one. The chains "want" to recoil simply to regain that arrangement-freedom (entropy). Even stranger: heat the stretched band and it pulls back *harder*, because the entropic restoring force grows with temperature — the opposite of a metal spring.

### Precisely

**Entropic elasticity** is the restoring force of a flexible polymer that arises from the *reduction in conformational entropy* upon stretching, not from bond strain. For an **ideal chain** of $N$ Kuhn segments of length $b$ at small extension $x$, the force is

$$f = \frac{3k_BT}{Nb^2}\,x,$$

a Hookean (linear) spring with stiffness $3k_BT/(Nb^2)$. Note the force is **proportional to temperature** $T$ — the hallmark of an entropic spring — and *softer* for longer chains (larger $N$).

### Worked example

A chain with $N=100$ Kuhn segments of $b=1$ nm has effective stiffness $3k_BT/(Nb^2) = 3k_BT/100\,\mathrm{nm^2}$. To extend it by $x=5$ nm at 300 K ($k_BT\approx4.1$ pN·nm): $f = 3\times4.1\times5/100 \approx 0.6$ pN — a sub-piconewton force, exactly the scale single-molecule **tweezers** measure. Stretch it further toward full extension and the force diverges nonlinearly (the **worm-like-chain** force law takes over).

### Why it's true / how it works

A coiled chain has a huge number of microscopic conformations; a stretched chain has far fewer (in the limit of full extension, just one). Free energy $F = -TS$ rises as stretching lowers the entropy $S$, and the restoring force is $f = \partial F/\partial x = -T\,\partial S/\partial x$. Because the energy of an *ideal* chain doesn't change with shape, the force is *purely* the entropy gradient — hence proportional to $T$.

### Where it connects

It is the mechanics of the **ideal/worm-like chain**, the molecular basis of rubber elasticity and **polymer gels** (network strands are entropic springs), and what single-molecule **optical/magnetic tweezers** and **AFM** pulling read out.

### Watch out

The linear $f\propto x$ law holds only at **small extension**; near full stretch the force shoots up steeply (the WLC regime), so don't extrapolate the Hookean form. And the temperature dependence is genuinely *opposite* to ordinary materials — entropic springs *stiffen* when heated, which trips up intuition built on metal springs.

### Numbers & nuance

The defining, counterintuitive signatures: the restoring force is **proportional to temperature** (heat a stretched rubber band and it contracts *harder* — opposite to a metal spring, which softens), and the stiffness $3k_BT/(Nb^2)$ is *softer* for longer chains. Forces are tiny — sub-piconewton at modest extension — exactly the scale single-molecule tweezers resolve. The linear (Hookean) law holds only at small extension; near full contour length the force diverges nonlinearly as the worm-like-chain force law $f\approx(k_BT/l_p)[\tfrac14(1-x/L)^{-2}-\tfrac14+x/L]$ takes over. This pure-entropy origin (the *ideal* chain has no shape-dependent energy, so $f=-T\,\partial S/\partial x$) is what makes rubber, the cytoskeleton, and stretched DNA all behave as entropic springs.

atoms.title: Polymer networks, gels & scaling
atoms.summary: Crosslinking polymer chains into a network produces a soft solid (a gel) whose elastic modulus is set by the density of network strands times k_BT — entropic elasticity scaled up to a material.

depths.eli5: Tie many floppy chains together at junctions and you get a squishy solid like jelly. Each connecting strand acts as a little entropic spring, so the whole network's stiffness comes from counting strands and temperature, not from strong bonds.
depths.core: In a crosslinked network, each strand between crosslinks is an entropic spring. Rubber-elasticity theory predicts a shear modulus G ≈ ν·k_BT, where ν is the number density of elastically active strands — so gels are soft (kPa) precisely because ν·k_BT is small. The sol–gel transition is a percolation phenomenon: as crosslinks accumulate, at a critical point a system-spanning network suddenly appears and the material switches from liquid (sol) to solid (gel).
depths.deep: Semidilute solutions introduce a correlation length (mesh size) ξ that controls what can diffuse through and how the osmotic modulus scales with concentration (de Gennes scaling laws, e.g. ξ ~ c^(−3/4) in good solvent). For stiff biopolymer networks (actin, collagen, intermediate filaments) the persistence length matters: they are strain-stiffening — the modulus rises sharply with strain as entropic slack runs out, a nonlinearity living cells exploit for mechanical robustness. The cytoskeleton, mucus, the extracellular matrix, and the nuclear pore's FG-mesh are all biological gels read through this lens.

atoms.note: Gel stiffness G ≈ ν·k_BT (strand density × thermal energy) is why biological gels are soft yet solid; the sol–gel transition is a percolation event, and stiff-chain networks 'strain-stiffen' (get harder the more you deform them). ('Sol' = a flowing liquid of separate chains; 'gel' = a connected solid network; 'percolation' = the moment scattered links first join into one spanning web.)
atoms.art_prompt: a crosslinked mesh of polymer strands forming a gel, each strand drawn as an entropic spring, a percolation threshold where a spanning network first appears, a strain-stiffening stress-strain curve

quiz.prompt: What sets the elastic (shear) modulus of a crosslinked polymer gel, and why are such gels soft?
quiz.answer: The shear modulus is approximately ν·k_BT, where ν is the number density of elastically active strands between crosslinks. Gels are soft because this product is small — the stiffness is entropic (k_BT per strand), not from strong bonds, and strand densities are modest.

quiz.prompt: Why is the sol–gel transition described as a percolation phenomenon?
quiz.answer: As crosslinks are added, clusters grow until, at a critical crosslink density, a single connected network spans the whole sample. That percolation threshold is where the material abruptly gains a static shear modulus — switching from a flowing liquid (sol) to an elastic solid (gel).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Take many floppy polymer chains and tie them together at random crosslinks. Each strand between crosslinks is a tiny entropic spring (it resists being stretched because stretching reduces its arrangement-freedom). Link enough of them into one connected web and you get a soft solid — a **gel** — like jelly or the inside of a cell. Its springiness is just the combined pull of countless molecular entropic springs, scaled up to a material you can hold.

### Precisely

A **polymer gel** is a crosslinked network of polymer strands swollen with solvent, forming a soft elastic solid. Its **shear modulus** (stiffness) is set by the number density of elastically active **network strands** $\nu$ times the thermal energy:

$$G \approx \nu\,k_BT,$$

so more crosslinks (more, shorter strands) means a stiffer gel, and stiffness *rises with temperature* — the signature of **entropic elasticity** at the material scale. Near the **gel point** (the critical crosslink density at which a system-spanning network first forms), properties follow universal **scaling** (power) laws.

### Worked example

A gel with strand density $\nu = 10^{25}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ has modulus $G \approx \nu k_BT = 10^{25}\times4\times10^{-21}\,\mathrm{J/m^3} \approx 4\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{Pa}$ — tens of kilopascals, a soft, jelly-like solid. Halve the crosslink density and you roughly halve the modulus: stiffness counts *strands*, each contributing ~$k_BT$ of entropic spring energy.

### Why it's true / how it works

Each network strand is an **entropic spring** with stiffness $\sim k_BT/(Nb^2)$. The macroscopic modulus is the energy density of these springs under deformation; counting strands per unit volume and multiplying by their per-strand $k_BT$ scale gives $G\sim\nu k_BT$ (**rubber elasticity theory**). The temperature dependence is inherited directly from the entropic origin of each strand's restoring force. At the **sol–gel transition**, the emergence of an infinite cluster is a **percolation** phenomenon with critical scaling exponents.

### Where it connects

It scales up **entropic elasticity** and the **ideal/worm-like chain** to bulk materials, underlies the cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix mechanics, hydrogels in bioengineering, and the **gel-like** material states of biomolecular **condensates**.

### Watch out

$G\sim\nu k_BT$ counts only **elastically active** strands — dangling ends and loops that don't bridge the network contribute nothing, so the *effective* strand density is below the total. And near the gel point the simple linear theory fails; behaviour is governed by **critical scaling**, not a fixed modulus.

### Numbers & nuance

The rubber-elasticity estimate $G\approx\nu k_BT$ counts only **elastically effective** strands (those bridging the network) — dangling ends and intramolecular loops contribute nothing, so the effective $\nu$ is below the nominal crosslink density. A gel with $\nu\sim10^{25}$ strands/m³ has $G\sim$ tens of kPa, soft like jelly or tissue. The temperature dependence (stiffer when warmer) inherits directly from each strand's entropic spring nature. Near the **sol–gel transition**, the first system-spanning cluster forms — a **percolation** phenomenon — and properties follow universal power-law scaling rather than the simple linear formula, with the modulus vanishing as the gel point is approached from above. Biological gels (cytoskeleton, mucus, extracellular matrix) and the gel-like states of condensates all obey this network elasticity.

atoms.title: Reaction–diffusion & Turing patterns
atoms.summary: Coupling chemical reactions to diffusion can spontaneously break spatial uniformity, generating stationary patterns — Turing's mechanism for how a uniform embryo can self-organize structure.

depths.eli5: Mix two chemicals that react and spread at different speeds, and a perfectly even soup can spontaneously develop spots or stripes. A short-range 'activator' builds itself up locally while a fast-spreading 'inhibitor' keeps it in check from afar.
depths.core: Turing (1952) showed that a stable, spatially uniform steady state of a reaction system can become unstable when diffusion is added — diffusion-driven instability. The classic recipe is a slowly-diffusing self-enhancing activator plus a fast-diffusing long-range inhibitor (local activation, lateral inhibition). Linearizing the two-species reaction–diffusion equations and analyzing the growth rate of each Fourier mode shows a band of finite wavelengths grows fastest, selecting a pattern with an intrinsic length scale set by reaction rates and diffusion constants.
depths.deep: Counterintuitively, diffusion — usually a homogenizing force — here destabilizes. The condition requires the inhibitor to diffuse substantially faster than the activator (D_inh ≫ D_act); the unstable wavenumber band comes from the eigenvalues of the linearized reaction Jacobian plus the −Dk² diffusion terms (an eigenmode/normal-mode analysis in space). Nonlinear saturation then sets the pattern's amplitude. Turing patterns plausibly underlie animal coat markings, digit spacing, hair-follicle arrays, and left–right symmetry breaking, though identifying the real morphogens has been hard — a triumph of physics predicting biology decades before molecules were found.

atoms.note: Diffusion-driven instability is the paradox: diffusion, which normally smooths things out, instead breaks uniformity when a fast 'inhibitor' outruns a slow 'activator'. The resulting spots/stripes have a built-in wavelength set by chemistry. ('Activator' = a substance that makes more of itself and the inhibitor; 'inhibitor' = a substance that suppresses the activator; 'morphogen' = a patterning chemical in a developing embryo.)

resources.label: Wikipedia — The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis (Turing's 1952 paper)
Wikipedia — Fick's laws of diffusion (the diffusion half)

atoms.art_prompt: a uniform field spontaneously developing spots and stripes, a short-range activator peak flanked by a broad fast-spreading inhibitor, a dispersion curve with a band of unstable wavenumbers

quiz.prompt: What is diffusion-driven (Turing) instability, and what relationship between activator and inhibitor diffusion does it require?
quiz.answer: It is the destabilization of a spatially uniform steady state by adding diffusion, generating a patterned state. It requires a self-enhancing activator that diffuses slowly and a long-range inhibitor that diffuses much faster (D_inhibitor ≫ D_activator) — local activation with lateral inhibition.

quiz.prompt: How does linear stability analysis predict the pattern's length scale?
quiz.answer: Linearize the reaction–diffusion equations about the uniform state and expand perturbations in Fourier modes e^(ikx); each mode's growth rate comes from the eigenvalues of the reaction Jacobian minus the Dk² diffusion terms. A finite band of wavenumbers k has positive growth rate, and the fastest-growing k sets the dominant wavelength of the emergent pattern.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

How does a uniform ball of identical cells in an embryo spontaneously develop stripes, spots, or a head-to-tail axis? Alan Turing's startling answer: chemistry plus diffusion alone can do it. If two chemicals react *and* spread at different speeds, a perfectly even mixture can become *unstable* and organize itself into a stationary pattern — peaks and valleys of concentration — with no external blueprint. Diffusion, usually a smoother-out, here becomes a pattern-*maker*.

### Precisely

A **reaction–diffusion** system couples chemical kinetics to spatial spreading:

$$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = f(u,v) + D_u\nabla^2 u,\qquad \frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = g(u,v) + D_v\nabla^2 v,$$

where $u,v$ are concentrations, $f,g$ the reaction terms, and $D_u,D_v$ diffusion coefficients. A **Turing instability** occurs when a uniform steady state is stable *without* diffusion but becomes *unstable* *with* it — classically requiring a slowly-diffusing **activator** and a fast-diffusing **inhibitor** ("local activation, long-range inhibition"). The instability selects a finite wavelength, giving stationary spots or stripes.

### Worked example

In the activator–inhibitor scheme, the activator $u$ promotes both itself and its inhibitor $v$; $v$ suppresses $u$ and diffuses *faster* ($D_v \gg D_u$). A small local bump in $u$ amplifies locally (autocatalysis) but, because the inhibitor races outward, surrounding regions are suppressed — locking in a peak here, a trough nearby, repeated at a characteristic spacing. That spacing is the pattern's wavelength, set by the ratio $D_v/D_u$ and the kinetics.

### Why it's true / how it works

Linearize about the uniform state and ask which spatial wavelengths grow. Without diffusion the state is stable (all perturbations decay). Adding unequal diffusion makes a *band* of intermediate wavelengths have positive growth rate — the fastest-growing one sets the pattern scale. It is a **diffusion-driven instability**: counterintuitively, the *difference* in diffusion rates is what breaks the symmetry.

### Where it connects

It extends **Fick's diffusion** by coupling it to reaction kinetics (**Michaelis–Menten**-like terms), generates the spatial patterns underlying **signal-transduction**-based development (morphogen gradients), and is a canonical example of **self-organization** and symmetry breaking.

### Watch out

The instability **requires unequal diffusion** — equal $D_u = D_v$ cannot produce Turing patterns; the activator must diffuse slower than the inhibitor. And while Turing's mechanism elegantly *can* explain biological patterns, demonstrating that a *particular* pattern (animal coats, digit spacing) is genuinely Turing-driven rather than produced by some other mechanism requires identifying the actual molecular species — a frequent over-claim.

### Numbers & nuance

The non-negotiable ingredient is **unequal diffusion**: a Turing instability needs a slow-diffusing **activator** and a fast-diffusing **inhibitor** ("local activation, long-range inhibition"); equal diffusion coefficients can never break symmetry. The instability selects a finite **wavelength** set by the geometric mean of reaction and diffusion scales, $\sim\sqrt{D/k}$, which fixes the spacing of spots or stripes independent of domain size — a hallmark of pattern *scaling*. The mechanism elegantly shows that diffusion, normally a homogenizer, can *create* structure. The honest caution: demonstrating a *specific* biological pattern (coat markings, digit spacing, hair follicles) is genuinely Turing-driven — rather than produced by positional-information gradients or mechanical mechanisms — requires identifying the actual molecular activator/inhibitor species, which is hard and often missing.

atoms.title: Optical & magnetic tweezers
atoms.summary: Single-molecule force spectroscopy: a trapped bead applies and measures piconewton forces on one molecule, reading out its mechanics, folding, and motor stepping in real time.

depths.eli5: A tightly focused laser (or a magnetic field) grabs a microscopic bead like invisible tweezers. Tie a single molecule to the bead and you can gently pull on it, measuring forces a trillion times smaller than a gram of weight.
depths.core: An optical trap is a tightly focused laser beam whose intensity gradient pulls a dielectric bead toward the focus; near the center the restoring force is Hookean, F = −k_trap·x, so measuring the bead's displacement reads out force (pN) with sub-nm precision. Tethering a DNA or protein between beads (or a bead and surface) lets you record force–extension curves — fit by the worm-like chain — and watch discrete folding/unfolding transitions or a motor's nanometer steps. Magnetic tweezers instead pull on a magnetic bead and naturally apply constant force and torque, ideal for studying DNA twist and topoisomerases.
depths.deep: The fundamental noise floor is thermal: the trapped bead jiggles with ⟨x²⟩ = k_BT/k_trap (equipartition), which both calibrates the trap stiffness and sets the force resolution and bandwidth tradeoff. Constant-force (force-clamp) versus constant-position (position-clamp) modes probe different ensembles; pulling at varying loading rates and applying Bell/Dudko–Hummer–Szabo theory extracts the energy landscape's barrier height and position from the distribution of rupture forces — turning mechanical pulling into a thermodynamic measurement of ΔG‡ and x‡.

atoms.note: Calibrating the trap is pure statistical mechanics: the equipartition rule ⟨x²⟩ = k_BT/k gives the stiffness, and the spread of rupture forces reveals the molecule's energy landscape (barrier height and position). ('Piconewton', pN, is a trillionth of a newton — the force scale of single molecules; 'equipartition' = each independent way of jiggling carries ½k_BT of energy on average.)

resources.label: Wikipedia — Worm-like chain (fits the force–extension curves)

atoms.art_prompt: a laser-focused bead held in a harmonic trap with a single DNA molecule tethered to a second bead, a worm-like-chain force-extension curve and discrete unfolding steps on a trace

quiz.prompt: How does an optical trap convert a bead's measured displacement into a force?
quiz.answer: Near the focus the trap acts as a harmonic (Hookean) spring, F = −k_trap·x, so the bead's displacement x from the trap center, multiplied by the calibrated stiffness k_trap, gives the applied force — typically in the piconewton range.

quiz.prompt: How is trap stiffness calibrated from thermal motion, and what does this imply for resolution?
quiz.answer: By equipartition, the trapped bead's mean-square thermal displacement satisfies ½k_trap⟨x²⟩ = ½k_BT, so k_trap = k_BT/⟨x²⟩ — measuring the bead's positional variance calibrates the stiffness. The same thermal jiggle is the noise floor, setting the fundamental force/spatial resolution and its tradeoff with bandwidth.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

You can grab a single molecule with a beam of light. Focus a laser tightly and it traps a tiny transparent bead at its brightest point, holding it like an invisible spring. Tether one end of a DNA or protein to that bead and the other to a surface, and you can pull on *one molecule* with forces of a few piconewtons — and simultaneously *measure* the force and the molecule's extension in real time, watching it stretch, fold, or a motor step along it.

### Precisely

**Optical tweezers** use a focused laser beam to trap a micron-sized dielectric bead: the light's intensity gradient exerts a restoring force, $F = -k_{\text{trap}}\,x$, that is **Hookean** near the focus (trap stiffness $k_{\text{trap}}$, displacement $x$). By tethering a single molecule between the bead and a surface (or a second trapped bead), one applies and reads out **piconewton** forces and **nanometre** extensions. **Magnetic tweezers** instead pull a magnetic bead with a field gradient and can also apply *torque* (twist).

### Worked example

Pull on a single DNA molecule and fit its **force–extension** curve to the **worm-like chain** model to extract its persistence length (~50 nm) and contour length. Or watch a **molecular motor** (kinesin) walk a tethered bead: the trace shows discrete ~8 nm steps, and increasing the load until the motor stalls measures its ~5–7 pN **stall force** — directly reading the motor's mechanics one molecule at a time.

### Why it's true / how it works

A transparent bead refracts the laser light; conservation of photon momentum produces a net force pulling the bead toward the highest intensity (the focus). Near the centre this force is linear in displacement, making a calibrated spring whose stiffness is set by laser power and bead size. Tracking the bead's position (to sub-nanometre precision) yields both force ($k_{\text{trap}}x$) and molecular extension.

### Where it connects

It is the experimental probe behind the **worm-like chain**, **entropic elasticity**, single-molecule folding (complementing **smFRET**), and **molecular-motor** stepping; it operates in the **overdamped Langevin** regime and resolves piconewton biology.

### Watch out

The trap is only **Hookean near its centre** — pull too far and the linear force calibration fails. Bead and tether introduce their own compliance, so the measured extension must be corrected for the linker. And the forces are tiny (pN): thermal noise on the bead is comparable, so signals require careful averaging and calibration.

### Numbers & nuance

Force/length scales: optical traps apply ~0.1–100 pN with sub-nanometre position resolution, ideal for the entropic, sub-pN regime of stretching DNA and watching motors step (kinesin's 8 nm steps, ~5–7 pN stall). The trap is a calibrated Hookean spring, $F=-k_{\text{trap}}x$, only *near* the focus — pull too far and the linear calibration breaks. Magnetic tweezers complement them by applying constant force *and* controlling **twist** (torque), uniquely suited to studying DNA supercoiling and topoisomerases. Both require correcting for linker/bead compliance, and because the forces are comparable to thermal noise on the bead, signals demand careful calibration (e.g. via the power spectrum of bead fluctuations) and averaging. Together they made single-molecule mechanics — folding, motors, nucleic-acid processing — directly observable.

atoms.title: Atomic force microscopy
atoms.summary: A sharp tip on a flexible cantilever feels single molecules: it images surfaces at nanometer resolution and mechanically unfolds proteins one domain at a time.

depths.eli5: Drag an incredibly sharp needle on a tiny diving board across a surface; as it rides up and down over bumps, a laser tracks the board's bending to build a height map fine enough to see single molecules. Hook the tip to a protein and pull, and you can rip it apart one piece at a time.
depths.core: AFM measures the deflection of a microcantilever (spring constant ~10–100 pN/nm) as its nanoscale tip interacts with a sample, read out by a laser bouncing off the cantilever onto a photodiode. In imaging mode it maps topography at sub-nm vertical resolution in air or liquid — even on live cells. In force-spectroscopy mode the tip grabs a molecule and retracts; unfolding a multidomain protein (e.g. titin) gives a characteristic sawtooth force–extension curve, each peak a domain rupture fit by the worm-like chain.
depths.deep: Like the optical trap, the cantilever's thermal fluctuations calibrate its stiffness via equipartition. AFM accesses higher forces (tens of pN to nN) than optical tweezers, making it the tool for strong unfolding events and receptor–ligand bond rupture, but with poorer force resolution. Dynamic force spectroscopy — measuring how rupture force grows with loading rate — applies Bell–Evans theory to extract the bond's intrinsic off-rate and the distance to the transition state, again converting a mechanical pull into landscape parameters. High-speed AFM now films conformational dynamics (e.g. myosin walking) at video rates.

atoms.note: The titin 'sawtooth' — evenly spaced force peaks, each one a single domain popping open — is the classic AFM single-molecule signature, fit by the worm-like chain. AFM reaches higher forces than optical tweezers but with coarser resolution. ('Cantilever' = a tiny flexible diving-board whose bending is read by a reflected laser; a 'domain' is one independently folding chunk of a protein.)
atoms.art_prompt: a sharp tip on a cantilever with a laser-photodiode readout scanning a surface, and a separate panel of a multidomain protein being stretched into a sawtooth force-extension curve

quiz.prompt: What does the characteristic sawtooth force–extension curve from AFM pulling on a multidomain protein represent?
quiz.answer: Each peak is the unfolding (rupture) of one structural domain; as the chain is stretched, domains pop open sequentially, each releasing slack that is then re-tensioned, producing repeated rises and drops fit by the worm-like chain model.

quiz.prompt: When would you choose AFM over optical tweezers for single-molecule force work?
quiz.answer: AFM accesses higher forces (tens of pN to nN) and stiffer probes, so it suits strong unfolding events and receptor–ligand bond rupture, plus topographic imaging; optical tweezers offer finer force resolution (sub-pN) for delicate, low-force measurements like motor stepping.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Imagine reading a surface the way a blind person reads Braille — by *touch*. Atomic force microscopy drags an ultra-sharp tip, mounted on a springy cantilever, across a sample. As the tip rides over bumps, the cantilever bends, and a laser bouncing off it reports the deflection. This builds a nanometre-resolution topographic map with no lenses at all — and the same tip can grab a single protein and yank it apart, measuring the force domain by domain.

### Precisely

**Atomic force microscopy (AFM)** scans a sharp tip on a flexible **cantilever** over a surface. The cantilever obeys Hooke's law, $F = -k_c\,d$ (spring constant $k_c$, deflection $d$), and its bending — sensed by a reflected laser on a photodiode — reports the tip–sample force. In **imaging** mode it maps surface topography at nanometre (sometimes atomic) resolution, in air or even in liquid. In **force-spectroscopy** mode the tip tethers a molecule and pulls, recording a **force–extension** curve.

### Worked example

Pull on a multidomain protein (e.g. titin) with AFM and the force trace shows a **sawtooth** pattern: force rises as a domain is stretched (entropic/WLC resistance), then drops sharply when one domain suddenly **unfolds** and releases length, then rises again for the next domain. Each peak's height (tens to hundreds of pN) measures that domain's mechanical stability, and the spacing measures the unfolded length per domain.

### Why it's true / how it works

The cantilever is a calibrated mechanical spring; measuring its deflection converts directly to force ($k_c d$). For imaging, a feedback loop keeps the force constant by raising/lowering the sample, and the height adjustments form the image. For pulling, the sequential unfolding peaks appear because each domain unravels cooperatively at its own threshold force, just like a series of **two-state** mechanical switches.

### Where it connects

AFM force spectroscopy reads **entropic elasticity** and the **worm-like chain**, probes mechanical (force-induced) **two-state folding/unfolding**, and complements **optical/magnetic tweezers** (AFM accesses higher forces, tens of pN to nN, vs tweezers' sub-pN to tens of pN). As imaging, it sits alongside **cryo-EM** and X-ray (**Bragg**) for structure.

### Watch out

AFM operates at **higher forces** and lower force-resolution than optical tweezers — they are complementary, not interchangeable. Imaging resolution is limited by **tip sharpness** (a blunt or contaminated tip blurs and can artificially broaden features), and soft biological samples can be deformed or damaged by the tip if the force isn't kept gentle.

### Numbers & nuance

AFM force spectroscopy accesses **higher forces** (tens of pN to nN) and stiffer cantilevers than optical tweezers, making it ideal for mechanically *unfolding* tough proteins like titin, whose sawtooth force–extension traces reveal each domain's unfolding force (often 100–300 pN) and unfolded length. Imaging resolution is set by **tip sharpness** (apex radius of a few nm); a blunt or contaminated tip convolutes with features and broadens them. AFM works in air *and* liquid, enabling imaging of live membranes and even real-time "high-speed AFM" movies of working molecular machines. The complementarity is the key takeaway: AFM for higher forces and surface imaging, optical/magnetic tweezers for the sub-pN entropic regime — choose the tool to match the force scale of the question.

atoms.title: Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS)
atoms.summary: Scattering at small angles from molecules in solution reports overall size, shape, and flexibility — low resolution but native, and uniquely powerful for disordered and multidomain proteins.

depths.eli5: Shine X-rays through a solution of molecules and look at how they scatter at very small angles. You can't see atoms, but you can measure how big and what general shape the molecules are — even floppy ones that won't crystallize.
depths.core: SAXS measures scattering intensity I(q) versus momentum transfer q for a dilute solution; because the molecules are randomly oriented, the signal is the orientationally-averaged form factor. The low-q Guinier regime gives the radius of gyration R_g (ln I(q) ≈ ln I(0) − q²R_g²/3), and I(0) scales with molecular mass. The full curve, and its real-space Fourier transform the pair-distance distribution P(r), encode overall shape, oligomeric state, and conformational ensembles — all in physiological solution, no crystal needed.
depths.deep: For flexible or disordered chains the scattering follows polymer scaling (the Kratky plot I·q² vs q distinguishes globular folds, which peak and fall, from unfolded chains, which plateau or rise) — a direct readout of compactness versus expansion. SAXS resolution is low (~1 nm), so it constrains rather than determines structure; it is most powerful combined with crystallography, NMR, or computation (rigid-body and ensemble modeling). Time-resolved SAXS follows folding and assembly in real time, and contrast variation (SANS with deuteration) isolates components in complexes.

atoms.note: Guinier analysis gives the size R_g, the Kratky plot reveals folded-vs-disordered, and P(r) gives the overall shape — all in solution, no crystal needed. SAXS is the go-to for the flexible, disordered molecules crystallography can't handle. ('Scattering' = light/X-rays bouncing off molecules in many directions; 'radius of gyration' R_g is a single number summarizing a molecule's spread-out size.)
